entries.title: Review: Jae Stephens deserves a larger stage — and more hearts to break — in Lollapalooza debut
entries.summary: <p>Jae Stephens makes music for heartbreakers.</p><p>That much was true for the Los Angeles-based pop and R&B singer during her Lollapalooza debut Saturday on the BMI stage, where she sang odes to keeping a roster of men for options — and loving and leaving without regard.</p><p>“Which one should I choose today? Switch ’em out like shoes today,” she sang on her single “SMH,” with a sly smile to the delight of the crowd, who erupted when Stephens brought out Chicago’s very own Shea Couleé to snap into fierce choreography alongside her.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5d0000" though Stephens’ was a little less tender — “I never save their numbers, just here for the summer,” she sang while popping on stage. And her song “Precious” had a bounce that conjured images of Ciara.</p><p>In response to the loud cheers for her, Stephens appeared to get emotional onstage, before clicking back into stunt mode.</p><p>Stephens and two backup dancers hit their marks, dedicating choreo to each song while Stephens kept singing without a hint of sounding winded, as if she trained at the Destiny’s Child academy for pop’s next big star.</p><p>In reality, Stephens, 29, has cut her teeth in the music industry and as a performer, releasing several mixtapes and writing songs for the likes of Jennifer Lopez.</p><p>Clocking in at just 30 minutes, Stephens felt deserving of a larger stage, longer set time and more hearts to break.</p>

entries.title: Review: Tate McRae closes out Lollapalooza with surprisingly subdued set
entries.summary: <p>Several songs into her headlining Lollapalooza set on Sunday night, Tate McRae pulled out a microphone stand to sing “Anything But Love,” as if to reiterate that she does, in fact, sing live in addition to performing high-energy choreography.</p><p>By no means a vocal dynamo, McRae is a competent singer, though audiences shouldn’t expect any vocal surprises. But the mic served as a symbol not of vocal prowess but an invitation to focus on McRae as a lyricist.</p><p>To her fans, she is not a manufactured pop star. Many of them have grown up with her since she began posting songs online as a teenager and resonate deeply with her lyrics, which often touch on heartbreak. They were likely happy with the set, which was surprisingly more subdued than expected.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" name="image-8f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f9d37b9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5359x3008+0+282/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F63%2Fb47fdbe348b291d1aacfe928fa23%2F186a3186.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a4a82d5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5359x3008+0+282/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F63%2Fb47fdbe348b291d1aacfe928fa23%2F186a3186.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5e0e34/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5359x3008+0+282/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F63%2Fb47fdbe348b291d1aacfe928fa23%2F186a3186.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Tate McRae performs Sunday on the T-Mobile stage on Day 4 of Lollapalooza. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5e0e34/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5359x3008+0+282/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F63%2Fb47fdbe348b291d1aacfe928fa23%2F186a3186.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/13d3298/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5359x3008+0+282/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F63%2Fb47fdbe348b291d1aacfe928fa23%2F186a3186.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5e0e34/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5359x3008+0+282/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F63%2Fb47fdbe348b291d1aacfe928fa23%2F186a3186.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Tate McRae performs Sunday on the T-Mobile stage on Day 4 of Lollapalooza.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But for casual viewers getting acquainted with her as a live performer, they may have left disappointed. entries.title: 3 hurt in 2-vehicle wreck on Edens Expressway in Northbrook
entries.summary: <p>Traffic was getting by on one shoulder after a collision on the Edens Expressway that left three people injured early Monday in Northbrook. </p><p>Around 4:50 a.m., state troopers responded to the outbound lanes near Dundee Road for a crash involving two vehicles, Illinois state police said. </p><p>Three people were hospitalized with injuries, officials said. </p><p>Outbound lanes were shut down with traffic getting by on the shoulder as of 7 a.m., state police said. </p><p>No further information was immediately available. </p>

entries.title: Printers Row Lit Fest 2026 will return Sept. 12-13
entries.summary: <p>The 41st annual Printers Row Lit Fest announced today its lineup of more than 200 authors, journalists, poets and screenwriters who will appear during the free event, which will take place Sept. 12-13.</p><p>Some Jewish authors have <a class="Link" href="https://forward.com/culture/books/841358/a-major-chicago-literary-festival-overlaps-with-rosh-hashanah-jewish-authors-are-dismayed-to-learn/" target="_blank" ><u>pointed out</u></a> that the event coincides with Rosh Hashanah, the High Holiday marking the Jewish New Year, but festival organizers said the scheduling was particularly challenging this year.</p><p>Headliners include Chicago author <b>Scott Turow</b>, a lawyer whose books “Presumed Innocent” and “The Burden of Proof” center around the legal world. Plus, broadcast journalist <b>Geoff Bennett</b>, the Peabody Award-winning co-host of PBS NewsHour, whose new book is “Black Out Loud. entries.title: 3-year-old girl, 3 cops among 5 hurt in Washington Park crash
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police on their way to a gun call collided with a car, leaving five people hurt including a 3-year-old girl and three Chicago police officers Sunday night in Washington Park on the South Side. </p><p>Officers in an unmarked car were responding to a call of a person with a gun around 9:30 p.m. and were going west near the 100 block of East 63rd Street when their vehicle collided with a white car going north, Chicago police said. </p><p>A 3-year-old girl inside the car suffered a fractured tibia and was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital, where she was listed in fair condition, police said.</p><p>A 41-year-old passenger in the sedan suffered a broken neck and was taken to Stroger Hospital in fair condition, police said. </p><p>Car's driver, a 32-year-old woman who declined medical attention, was cited for speeding and having no insurance. </p><p>Three officers suffered "minor" injures and were taken to area hospitals in fair condition, officials said.<br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Husband is carrying the world on his shoulders
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been with my wife for 17 years. We have three daughters. She doesn't work, doesn't have a driver's license, doesn't clean and rarely cooks. I often find myself so frustrated at her lack of commitment to the family that I drink and go to bed after I cook dinner.</p><p>I work 60 hours a week to provide for our family and am not receiving any help from my wife. I don't know what to do. I do all the shopping and take the girls to dance three days a week (which means I have to leave work early). It causes bad arguments. What can I do to motivate her to change? <i>— DOING EVERYTHING IN NEW HAMPSHIRE</i> </p><p><b>DEAR DOING EVERYTHING:</b> You state that your wife doesn't work, doesn't drive, doesn't clean and rarely cooks. What does she do all day? Is she watching television? Taking drugs? Is she so depressed she can't get out of bed?</p><p>You should not be carrying the whole load yourself, but drinking and going to bed are not the answer. Ask your doctor or health insurance company for a referral to a licensed psychotherapist who can help you unravel this mess. Nothing will change until you do.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My daughter added her girlfriend to our family group chat last December. Now the girlfriend is accepting invitations from family members that weren't meant for her. Granted, she has been dating my daughter for more than five years, but none of us like her or feel comfortable around her. We're afraid to say anything due to our love for our daughter. How do we get her off the family group chat and stop her from being so invasive in our lives without hurting our daughter? <i>— CLOSING RANKS</i> </p><p><b>DEAR CLOSING RANKS:</b> No matter what you do about the group chat, the end result will have to be a conversation with your daughter about the fact that her girlfriend is not welcome at certain family gatherings. Are you willing to have that talk and face the consequences? If not, it might be best to learn to get along with the girlfriend and remember that most people do not get to pick their in-laws. </p><p>If you are determined that excluding the girlfriend is the way to go, start a new group chat and emphasize to your daughter that this one is for immediate family only.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> When my husband passed away, his sister "Enid" and her husband, "Fred," did not attend his funeral. Their grown son and daughter with grown children of their own also missed the funeral. They claimed Fred had a doctor's appointment. This made a total of 10 people unable to come to the funeral. We all live in the same area, so there was no traveling involved. What is your opinion about me being upset? <i>— BOTHERED IN THE EAST</i> </p><p><b>DEAR BOTHERED:</b> First, please accept my deepest sympathy for the loss of your husband. You have a right to be upset about Enid, Fred and their family skipping your husband's funeral. A doctor's appointment can usually be rescheduled. Funerals are a different matter. The fact is, they chose to withhold their support from you, which was thoughtless, bordering on cruel. </p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Grant Park Music Festival strikes the right chords
entries.summary: <p>The recent <a class="Link" href="https://loopchicago.com/press-releases/world-class-experiences-and-billions-in-investment-drive-loops-q2-economy/" target="_blank" >Chicago Loop Alliance report</a> on the economic benefits of arts and culture to Chicago highlights a simple but important truth — cultural institutions do more than entertain.</p><p>They help define Chicago’s identity, strengthen communities, draw visitors from all corners of the world and generate meaningful economic activity.</p><p>For nearly a century, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.grantparkmusicfestival.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23810822549&gbraid=0AAAAA9pYp6INBSy2gV-hDYn5g63NftQg3&gclid=Cj0KCQjw94bTBhDQARIsAN3vv0y5gicWi_l1psKalFVyDSxabG8QDNE08SRTBeFO2YhDEbSUfIzo1_QaAmTpEALw_wcB" target="_blank" >Grant Park Music Festival</a> has embodied those benefits. One of the nation’s oldest, premier free outdoor classical music festivals, it is a cherished Chicago tradition and an essential part of Chicago’s cultural fabric. Each summer, over 300,000 people gather in Millennium Park to experience world-class music against the backdrop of our iconic skyline.</p><p>The festival’s impact extends well beyond the stage, generating over $20 million in economic activity each season and roughly $4 million in tax revenue to bolster Chicago coffers. While here contributing to Downtown's overall vitality, many out-of-town festival attendees support local restaurants, hotels, retailers and transportation services.</p><p>Through its world-class orchestra and chorus, the Grant Park Music Festival also employs nearly 300 professional musicians, helping retain exceptional artistic talent in Chicago and strengthening the broader creative economy. Beyond Millennium Park, these musicians perform in city neighborhoods, inspiring future generations through programs expanding access to the arts.</p><p>Reports like the Loop Alliance study confirm what Chicagoans have long understood: Investment in arts and culture yields tangible returns for our economy and our quality of life.</p><p>The value of cultural institutions like the Grant Park Music Festival runs deeper, creating shared civic experiences, bringing people from different backgrounds together and showcasing the very best of Chicago.</p><p>As Chicago continues to chart its future, we should recognize the Grant Park Music Festival not only as a cultural treasure, but as a proven civic and economic asset that will continue to benefit Chicago for generations. This fall, I look forward to joining this nearly century-old legacy and building on this civic asset for years to come.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.grantparkmusicfestival.com/news-stories/anwar-nasir-named-president-and-ceo/#:~:text=The%20Grant%20Park%20Music%20Festival%20is%20pleased%20to%20announce%20the,summer%2Fearly%20fall%20of%202026." target="_blank" ><i>Anwar Nasir,</i></a><i> president and CEO designate, Grant Park Music Festival</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b10000" name="module-b10000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Advocating for HBCU law schools</h3><p>I was raised between two places: the South Side of Chicago and Alabama, where my<br>family's roots run deep. Both taught me that Black institutions have always done more with less, and that the people inside them rarely get credit for it.</p><p>That lesson now comes full circle. I'm a third-year law student at the University of the District of Columbia <a class="Link" href="https://law.udc.edu/" target="_blank" >David A. Clarke</a> School of Law, and the first historically Black college and university law student ever elected to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanbar.org/groups/leadership/aba_officers/hawk-marc/" target="_blank" >American Bar Association’s Board of Governors</a>. I'll be in my hometown this week, standing before the ABA House of Delegates as the author and floor speaker for two resolutions: one that addresses the chronic underfunding of the nation's six ABA-accredited HBCU law schools, and one that urges Congress to cap runaway interest on student debt for attorneys who choose public service careers.</p><p>The numbers are hard to ignore. HBCU law schools make up roughly<a class="Link" href="https://racism.org/articles/basic-needs/education/47-education-legal-education/10543-black-an" target="_blank" > 3% of ABA-accredited institutions</a>, yet HBCU graduates <a class="Link" href="https://uncf.org/the-latest/how-hbcu-curricula-are-evolving-to-prepare-students-for-the-future-workforce" target="_blank" >account for</a> roughly 80% of the nation's Black judges and half of all Black lawyers. That success resulted in spite of chronic underfunding — not because of it. Meanwhile, the average law graduate now carries <a class="Link" href="https://educationdata.org/average-law-school-debt" target="_blank" >well over $130,000</a> in debt — a burden that pushes talented graduates away from public defense and civil rights work and toward whatever pays the loans down fastest.</p><p>This vote for the resolutions is taking place as the <a class="Link" href="https://educationdata.org/average-law-school-debt" target="_blank" >ABA faces pressure</a> to repeal its own diversity accreditation standard. That makes it more important that HBCU law schools have a voice in the room this week in the city that raised me.</p><p>Chicago taught me that institutions built by necessity, on the South Side and across the<br>Black Belt, don't ask for charity. They ask to be seen for what they've already delivered.</p><p><i>Marc J. Hawk III, University of the District of Columbia David A. Clarke School of Law, Class of 2027</i></p><h3>Environmental inequality a factor in heat-related deaths</h3><p>Chicago should treat heat deaths as an environmental warning, not just a public health tragedy. At least <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/30/westchester-man-died-from-heat-stress-autopsy-finds" >nine people died</a> from heat-related causes in Cook County last month, and the burden has fallen hardest on South, Southwest or West sides, where residents are more exposed to the urban heat island effect. </p><p>Cities create hotter conditions when they replace trees and soil with pavement, roofs and other heat-absorbing surfaces, and that built environment can make extreme weather far more dangerous.</p><p>Response to extreme heat cannot be limited to cooling centers and emergency alerts. Chicago should be investing much more aggressively in tree canopy, reflective surfaces, green roofs and neighborhood-scale cooling infrastructure.</p><p>If Chicago is serious about climate resilience, it has to treat heat as part of the city’s environmental design problem. Heat deaths are not just the result of high temperatures — they are the result of a city that doesn't have enough protection against those temperatures. Let's aim to reduce the heat island effect to keep people from dying.</p><p><i>Sandeep Pant, 11th grader, Palatine High School</i></p><h3>Idling on immigration</h3><p>Who is to blame for the immigration mess? Could it be that Congress — Democrats and Republicans — have been kicking the can down the road for the past 50 or 60 years?</p><p><i>Robert Bishop, Skokie</i></p><h3>Obama turns 65</h3><p>Sixty-five years ago, the then not-so-well-known future husband of South Sider Michelle Robinson was born.</p><p>He was the son of aspiring college students who the world now knows as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/24/obama-wnba-all-star-game-changemaker" >Barack Obama.</a></p><p>Years later, by some lucky chance, Robinson experienced a cordial professional relationship with this gentleman born in Hawaii.</p><p>They eventually married as Obama worked his way into the very essence of Chicagoland.</p><p>On Tuesday, Aug. 4, let's wish the former president a heartfelt happy 65th birthday.</p><p>Happy Birthday, President Obama. </p><p><i>Wayne E. Williams, Camden, New Jersey</i><br></p>

entries.title: If Chicago wants more housing, it should remove barriers to building
entries.summary: <p>Chicago is converting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/15/loop-building-residential-wave-office-conversions" target="_blank" >25</a> Downtown office buildings to apartments this year — more such projects than the city has seen in the past 20 years combined, the Sun-Times reported in June.</p><p>This is welcome news, and we need more of it. Bloomberg and Axios have reported that Chicago rents are up more than 35% since before the pandemic, which outpaces other major cities over the same period.</p><p>Despite demand, these conversion projects struggle to launch in Chicago because developers face expensive affordability requirements, unnecessary building codes and excessive aldermanic power. Chicago leaders must remove these structural barriers that make Downtown conversions challenging in order to meaningfully add to the city’s housing supply.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-110000" name="module-110000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Commercial-to-residential conversions can be completed <a class="Link" href="https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2025-nyc-midtown-office-conversions/" target="_blank" >faster</a> than projects starting from the ground up. Vacant offices are often near transit, jobs and amenities that make them desirable locations and ideal for tenants. Turning commercial corridors into mixed-use districts can make Downtown feel like a community, not just a workplace.</p><p>When the COVID-19 pandemic began, Chicago’s Downtown office vacancy rate hovered around <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/real-estate/commercial/ccb-downtown-office-vacancy-q1-20260406/" target="_blank" >13.8%</a>, according to Crain's Chicago Business. It reached <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/real-estate/commercial/ccb-downtown-office-vacancy-second-quarter-20260708/" target="_blank" >28%</a> recently, a slight dip from the 28.6% record high it hit in the first quarter of 2026.</p><p>The 25 projects underway Downtown will replace around 4 million square feet of vacant office space with over 3,900 units of housing. It’s a good start. Researchers estimate the state needs to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/06/24/illinois-chicago-housing-shortage-report/" target="_blank" >double</a> its current production rates to keep up with demand.</p><h3>Not worth the hassle</h3><h3></h3><p>Commercial-to-residential conversions frequently don’t “pencil out,” David Lapidus, a mid-rise, mixed-use developer and housing advocate in Chicago, told me.</p><p>“Until recently, the economics just didn’t work,” he said. “Between all the death-by-a-thousand-cuts city requirements related to zoning or building code, it just wasn’t worth the hassle.”</p><p>One of the biggest challenges to housing development in Chicago has been the Affordable Requirements Ordinance, which mandates that a certain percentage of units in new multifamily housing developments be rent-capped for at least 30 years. </p><p>In an <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoispolicy.org/reports/mandating-unaffordability-how-chicagos-housing-affordability-requirements-decrease-supply-and-increase-costs/" target="_blank" >analysis</a> I completed with a colleague at Illinois Policy, we estimated that restrictions created by the Affordable Requirements Ordinance and related regulations discouraged housing development and left Chicago with roughly 43,600 fewer potential market-rate housing units between 2016 and 2023 than it otherwise could have added. <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoispolicy.org/reports/mandating-unaffordability-how-chicagos-housing-affordability-requirements-decrease-supply-and-increase-costs/" target="_blank" ></a></p><p>Commercial-to-residential conversions frequently need zoning adjustments, which trigger the affordable requirements. By restricting the rent that can be collected on units in pricey neighborhoods, without adequate relief from other government programs for developers, the Affordable Requirements Ordinance reduces a project’s expected financial return.</p><p>“Developers are going to have more trouble raising equity or justifying the project on a risk-adjusted basis in general over many potential projects,” Lapidus said, noting the program's effects run opposite its "noble equity" goals.</p><p>If Chicago wants more housing, solving the financial challenges for developers — such as by scaling back or eliminating the Affordable Requirements Ordinance — will be critical.</p><h3>Complicated building codes</h3><h3></h3><p>These financial challenges are amplified by Chicago’s complicated, expensive and frequently unnecessary building codes.</p><p>Lapidus said he worked on a five-story conversion to residential years ago in Chicago’s Loop that was tall enough to trigger elevator requirements but not large enough to easily absorb the added cost of the larger and overbuilt elevator systems required by city and state codes. In <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/08/opinion/elevator-construction-regulation-labor-immigration.html?unlocked_article_code=1.11A.DXjw.LtD1knCSnmKG&smid=url-share" target="_blank" >Europe</a>, less onerous<a class="Link" href="https://admin.centerforbuilding.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Elevators.pdf" target="_blank" > elevator code requirements</a> are more common for mid-rise buildings.</p><p>Complications with Chicago and Illinois elevator codes “made that very challenging and added a lot of cost and lost a lot of potential usable residential square footage for the project,” while the inspection process added delays and requirements beyond what had been included in the original scope of work, with “unclear benefit for the public,” Lapidus said.</p><p>Changes to the building codes could remove complications and reduce costs on many fronts.</p><p>For example, developers aren’t allowed to use <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/content/dam/city/depts/bldgs/general/interpretations/P7-2021-001.pdf" target="_blank" >PVC pipe</a> for drain, waste and vent in projects over 60 feet in Chicago. Until 2021, they weren’t permitted to use it at all, forcing them to turn to expensive copper or cast iron pipes that Lapidus said could add 5% to the project cost.</p><p>Chicago is <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/06/04/is-one-way-out-enough-city-considers-building-code-change-to-address-housing-shortage/" target="_blank" >considering</a> building code reforms that would introduce more flexibility, but they’re mostly aimed at new developments. Code revisions that remove regulations affecting commercial conversions and large developments are important to appreciably increase housing.</p><p>Finally, Lapidus said, aldermanic preferences can still lead to projects not being allowed to proceed. Chicago has a long-standing tradition of “aldermanic prerogative,” meaning the local alderperson generally can nix any development plans in their ward.</p><p>“The alders are very, very powerful,” Lapidus said. “They can essentially have planning veto on most projects in their ward.” Alderpersons who don’t want commercial conversions in their ward find a way to prevent them based on “neighborhood character.”</p><p>By restricting those kinds of conversions with aldermanic prerogative, Chicago is undermining its own affordable-housing goals.</p><p>Between the ineffective affordability requirements, burdensome building codes and bureaucratic holdups, it is clear that the biggest obstacle to housing abundance in Chicago is the city itself.</p><p><i>LyLena D. Estabine is the senior policy analyst at the Illinois Policy Institute.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fb0000" name="module-fb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: LyLena D. Estabine

entries.title: Many women with high-risk pregnancies can’t get abortions in their home states. Illinois welcomes them.
entries.summary: <p>As states across much of the South and Midwest banned or further restricted abortions after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v Wade in 2022, they fueled a wave of people with high-risk pregnancies traveling to hospitals in Chicago.</p><p>The prohibitions also spurred a group of doctors, hospitals, a nonprofit and the state of Illinois to try to make a challenging and expensive journey a little easier.</p><p>“We’re really viewed as … one of the places of last resort,” said Dr. Laura Laursen, an OB/GYN at Rush University Medical Center who helped start what’s known as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2023/07/31/illinois-launching-hotline-for-high-risk-abortion-help" target="_blank" ><u>the Complex Abortion Regional Line for Access</u></a>, or <a class="Link" href="https://www.carlaprogram.org/" target="_blank" ><u>CARLA</u></a>, in 2023 to help women with high-risk pregnancies get abortion care in an Illinois hospital.</p><p>Even before <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2022/06/24/1102305878/supreme-court-abortion-roe-v-wade-decision-overturn" target="_blank" ><u>Roe fell</u></a>, Dr. Jonah Fleisher, an OB/GYN at UI Health, said women had to navigate a dizzying array of logistics to find an appointment.</p><p>He <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2023/06/28/illinois-hospitals-see-influx-of-high-risk-abortion-patients-from-out-of-state" target="_blank" ><u>would field calls</u></a> from panicked patients in parking lots of abortion clinics. They had just learned ending their pregnancies there would be too risky. They were handed a list of hospitals to call.</p><p>“They had already planned for weeks and sometimes even months to get that appointment, raise the funds, arrange for child care, time off of work, transportation — all the things to get to that appointment, whether from in state or out of state,” Fleisher said.</p><p>Hoping to streamline that process after Roe fell, Gov. JB Pritzker’s administration helped <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2023/07/31/illinois-launching-hotline-for-high-risk-abortion-help" target="_blank" ><u>launch CARLA</u></a>. Three years later, the need has remained steady, said Fleisher, who co-directs the program with Laursen.</p><p>CARLA receives about 40 referrals a week from around the country — around 1,500 referrals total over the past three years, including from Illinois. Women have come from more than 25 states.</p><p>The nonprofit Chicago Abortion Fund has pledged about $3 million for medical expenses and other support, such as travel costs.</p><h3>Illinois is considered a haven</h3><p>Illinois has some of the <a class="Link" href="https://states.guttmacher.org/policies/illinois/abortion-policies" target="_blank" ><u>strongest legal protections</u></a> in the nation for patients seeking abortions and for doctors who provide them.</p><p>More people travel to Illinois than to any other state for an abortion, according to the Guttmacher Institute, a nonprofit research and policy organization that tracks abortions and supports reproductive rights. In 2025, just more than 140,000 women traveled to other states to end their pregnancies; nearly 1 in 4 came to Illinois, <a class="Link" href="https://www.guttmacher.org/report/full-year-estimates-show-overall-stability-abortion-incidence-decreased-travel-increased-telehealth-provision" target="_blank" ><u>according to Guttmacher</u></a>.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2023/06/28/illinois-hospitals-see-influx-of-high-risk-abortion-patients-from-out-of-state" target="_blank" ><u>small percentage</u></a> of women seek abortions in hospitals, data shows. They’re typically higher risk — they have heart issues, conditions that make anesthesia more risky, or have a history of hemorrhaging — and need more medical resources than they can get at an outpatient clinic, doctors say.</p><p>Several patients who are referred to CARLA have a condition where the placenta grows too deeply into the wall of the uterus. It’s more common for women who have had a previous C-section, Fleisher said. A person can have serious bleeding during an abortion, and sometimes the only way to control the bleeding is a hysterectomy, he said.</p><p>Through CARLA, doctors from around the country call a hotline and refer patients to a team of nurses and physicians in Chicago, who help coordinate appointments for patients at four health systems. They are UI Health, Rush, Northwestern Medicine and UChicago Medicine.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-280000" name="image-280000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fb9f077/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7764x4357+0+409/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F4c%2F1e47522a42729f7611d7eaaa5d8c%2Fdsc-1711.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8d369fd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7764x4357+0+409/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F4c%2F1e47522a42729f7611d7eaaa5d8c%2Fdsc-1711.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3a89a9e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7764x4357+0+409/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F4c%2F1e47522a42729f7611d7eaaa5d8c%2Fdsc-1711.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="WBEZ - Monaghan/For WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Chicago Abortion Fund, known as CAF, can pick up the cost if patients can’t afford to. Since CARLA started, CAF has pledged to cover nearly $2 million in medical expenses for patients with complex medical needs, such as doctor appointments, hospital procedures and advanced ultrasound imaging.</p><p>The average hospital bill for patients seeking abortions is a few thousand dollars but can be far more expensive depending on the level of care. That’s compared to $500 to $1,000 for an abortion at an outpatient clinic.</p><p>Just 4% of CAF callers are people with complex medical needs who receive care in a hospital. But hospital bills make up about 25% of all of CAF’s spending on abortion care, compared to about 1.5% before Roe was overturned, said Meghan Daniel, senior director of programs at CAF.</p><p>The organization also pledged to cover another $1 million related to logistics for these patients, from airplane tickets to childcare.</p><p>In the first year of CARLA, about 40% of referrals were for out-of-state patients, compared to about 50% now, Fleisher said. More patients later in their pregnancies are being referred to the program, he said. It’s a sign that patients can’t get access in their home state, or something might have changed during their pregnancies, from a fetal diagnosis to losing their home or job, he said.</p><p>“I think people, to some degree, always had this need,” Fleisher said. “There just wasn't access.”</p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch is a senior reporter covering public health for WBEZ.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/stories/illinois-hospitals-see-influx-of-high-risk-abortion-patients-from-out-of-state/b8005315-8983-43fe-86a2-f841265237d4" >Abortion bans are fueling a rise in high-risk patients heading to Chicago hospitals</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2023/07/31/illinois-launching-hotline-for-high-risk-abortion-help" >Illinois Gov. entries.title: Bears S Coby Bryant carted off from practice with apparent knee injury
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> hit their first significant issue in training camp Monday when starting safety <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/18/bears-safeties-coby-bryant-dillon-thieneman-develop-tandem-bank-seattle-seahawks-oregon-purdue-ben-johnson" >Coby Bryant</a> left practice with an apparent knee injury.</p><p>About midway through practice, Bryant landed uncomfortably while covering tight end Cole Kmet in a one-on-one drill. He slammed his helmet down in frustration, and teammates came over to check on him as he grabbed his left knee before he left on a cart.</p><p>Being carted off is not necessarily cause for concern given that the Bears were practicing on the fields farthest from Halas Hall. Any injured player would exit that way. The bigger concern was that it was a non-contact injury and he reacted so emphatically to it.</p><p>Bryant, 27, was the Bears' top offseason acquisition, coming as a free agent from the defending champion Seahawks on a three-year, $40 million contract. The team has been counting on him to lead a defensive turnaround after it struggled last season.</p><p>Bryant has been a strong candidate to be a team captain as well, and the Bears could use a voice like his after letting Kevin Byard leave in free agency.</p><p>The Bears are especially thin at safety, where Bryant is the starter alongside first-round pick Dillon Thieneman.</p><p>Elijah Hicks would be in line behind them, but he's been out of camp with what the Bears have categorized as a minor shin injury. The Bears also have an option in Cam Lewis, who can play safety or corner and stepped into Bryant's spot for the rest of practice.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Why the Bears shouldn't play Caleb Williams in preseason games this year
entries.summary: <p>This is the third time in 12 years the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will have the same head coach, offensive play-caller and starting quarterback working together as they did the year before.</p><p>They should act like it.</p><p>The team’s first preseason game is less than two weeks away. If history is any indication, quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/01/bears-qb-caleb-williams-must-keep-climbing-no-matter-how-it-goes-with-offensive-line-this-season" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> won’t play in it. If common sense has any say, the same will be true of the Bears’ next two exhibition games.</p><p>Williams was seemingly everywhere this offseason, from hype lists to video game covers. Bears fans should hope the opposite is true this preseason.</p><p>There’s no reason to play Williams in games. That’s not a declaration that Williams is a finished product. Far from it — the Bears have a specific list of traits they absolutely need him to improve before the Sept. 13 opener in Charlotte, and certainly before they decide to play him like a franchise quarterback. Rather, holding Williams out of preseason games would be the reward for the quarterback and coach Ben Johnson establishing their on-field chemistry last year. Risking injury for the sake of more reps just doesn’t make sense.</p><p>Johnson wasn’t ready to lay out his game plan Monday for the Bears’ Aug. 15 preseason opener against the Browns at Soldier Field. But he didn’t commit to playing Williams, or any of his starters, in the opener.</p><p>The stretching portion before the game might be something different. Of course, there are no defenders trying to rip you to the ground then.</p><p>“I think it's probably always good to at least go through the warmup procedure to where Game 1’s not the first time at doing that,” Johnson said before Monday’s practice. “So there's a lot of merit in that regard, and we'll see what it looks like. But we haven't made a determination yet.”</p><p>The schedule seems to indicate otherwise. The Bears have a practice scheduled for the day after their first preseason game, the same way they did last year. Williams didn’t play the first preseason game in 2025, and neither did the majority of the Bears’ starters.</p><p>The next two preseason games — Aug. 22 in Cincinnati and Aug. 29 in Nashville — each come two days after a joint practice. Johnson figures to put more stock in practices against the Bengals and Titans, given that he’d have more control over the injury risk than in a game,</p><p>“We need all these guys to be as healthy as we possibly can going into the season because it's a long year,” Johnson said. “But at the same time, we want to make sure that we're prepped and we're ready also. We're looking at numbers. We got sports science data, the number of reps we're getting, the quality of the reps that we're getting, it all goes into it.”</p><p>The Bears played Williams in 14 snaps in the second preseason game last year and 28 in Game 3. But that was his first time working with Johnson, and he was still in the process of learning not only the playbook, but the presnap protocol. He knows both this year.</p><p>Johnson has stressed toughness since his arrival, but that’s built on practice fields, not random Saturdays in August The Bears will scrimmage during training camp and figure to have at least one repeat of last year’s grueling, violet showdown practices. That should be enough.</p><p>“It’s going to be a demanding ordeal,” Johnson said. “Anything worth doing is going to be challenging.”“It’s going to be a demanding ordeal,” Johnson said. “Anything worth doing is going to be challenging.”“It’s going to be a demanding ordeal,” Johnson said. “Anything worth doing is going to be challenging.”</p><p>“It’s going to be a demanding ordeal,” Johnson said. “Anything worth doing is going to be challenging.”</p><p>The Bears have been here before. Entering his second season with Mitch Trubisky, coach Matt Nagy decided to keep him on ice in the preseason. He didn’t throw a single pass. The Bears were beaten by the Packers in an ugly Week 1 and stumbled through 2019. Nagy, a year later, said he regretted not playing Trubisky more.</p><p>Williams isn’t Trubisky — at least the Bears hope not. And they hope Johnson has a staying power than Nagy never found.</p><p>They can’t decide Williams’ playing time this preseason based on the ghosts of quarterbacks past. Johnson and Williams, after all, are trying to break that mold.</p><p>“We'll be smart,” Johnson said.</p>

entries.title: Woman killed in Lynwood hit-and-run
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the driver of a vehicle that hit and killed a pedestrian in south suburban Lynwood early Monday. </p><p>Just after midnight, the woman was in the southbound lanes of Illinois 394 at Joe Orr Road in Lynwood when she was struck by a vehicle that didn’t stop, Illinois state police said. </p><p>The woman was taken to an area hospital where she was pronounced dead, state police said. Her name has not been released. </p><p>The roadway was shut down for an investigation and reopened just before 4 a.m., officials said. <br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Registration opens for Chicago Park District fall programs
entries.summary: <p>Registration for fall programs for the Chicago Park District opens Monday morning. </p><p>Beginning at 9 a.m., in-person programs are eligible for online registration at locations west of California Avenue. All virtual programs will also be available. </p><p>Starting Tuesday, those interested can sign up online for programs at locations east of California Avenue and gymnastics centers. </p><p>Most of the programs will run between Sept. 8 and Dec. 13. </p><p>More information can be found on the park district’s website. </p>

entries.title: White Sox add to bullpen with 36-year-old right-hander Huascar Brazoban
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox added to their bullpen overnight, acquiring right-hander Huascar Brazoban from the Mets for Double-A righty Gabe Davis and Triple-A righty Zach Franklin. Davis is the 18th-ranked prospect in the Sox' system, according to MLB.com.</p><p>Brazoban, 36, has a 2.56 ERA in 46 games this season, only his fifth in the major leagues. He has 49 strikeouts and 23 walks in 52 2/3 innings. He's under club control through 2030.</p><p>The Sox' bullpen is in flux. They traded right-handed reliever Seranthony Dominguez in the deal with the Mariners for righty starter Luis Castillo and moved righty Erick Fedde into the bullpen. Brazoban has a 96-97 mph fastball and a ground-ball percentage of 52.6%, thanks to his sinker, but his changeup is his best pitch. </p><p>Davis, a fifth-round draft pick in 2025, has a 5.81 ERA in 18 starts this season at High-A Winston-Salem and Double-A Birmingham. Franklin has a 4.37 ERA and five saves in 33 outings at Charlotte.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Motorcyclist hospitalized after collision with semi on Edens Expressway in Skokie
entries.summary: <p>A motorcyclist was hurt in a crash with a semi Monday morning on the outbound Edens Expressway in north suburban Skokie. </p><p>Just after 7 a.m., state troopers responded to the outbound lanes of Interstate 94 at Dempster Street for the crash and the motorcyclist was hospitalized with injuries, Illinois state police said. </p><p>No road closures were immediately reported. </p>

artist, she wanted to be a marine biologist.</p><p>So when she was commissioned to paint the viaduct at DuSable Lake Shore Drive and Fullerton Avenue, she called experts at the Shedd Aquarium for insight on native Lake Michigan flora and fauna, and invasive critters, too.</p><p>The result is a massive spread in Lincoln Park that celebrates Lake Michigan's natural history and intersects with entries.title: Wishbone closing after 36 years, co-owners announce
entries.summary: <p>Wishbone Chicago is closing its doors after 36 years, the West Loop restaurant's co-owners announced Monday morning. </p><p>"There is no easy way to say goodbye to something that has been such a large part of our lives for so long," Joel and Julie Nickson said in the Instagram announcement. "To our many loyal customers and to the generations of staff members who helped make Wishbone what it became, thank you."</p><p>The restaurant opened in 1990 at 1800 W. Grand Ave., moved to 1001 W. Washington Blvd. for 26 years and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/6/15/18445262/wishbone-has-found-a-new-west-loop-home" target="_blank" >moved again</a> to 161 N. Jefferson St. near Fulton Market in 2018. </p><p>The restaurant did not announce its last day of operation, but said it hopes to remain open through the end of August. </p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>

entries.title: White Sox get outfielder Brenton Doyle from Rockies for two prospects, including pitcher Mason Adams
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox are acquiring two-time Gold Glove center fielder Brenton Doyle from the Rockies, adding a right-handed bat to a left-handed-heavy unit. Right-hander Mason Adams, the eighth-ranked prospect in the Sox' system, according to MLB.com, and infielder Carlos Vielma are heading to the Rockies. </p><p>Doyle, 28, is slashing .214/.287/.282 with one home run in 45 games this season. He returned Friday from an oblique injury that cost him two months. His best season was in 2024, when he hit 23 homers, stole 30 bases and had an OPS+ of 102. Though his defensive metrics are down, too, Doyle is capable of playing elite defense. </p><p>He's owed $911,790 of his $3.1 million salary for the rest of the season and is under club control through 2029.</p><p>The Sox have left-handed hitters Sam Antonacci and Tristan Peters in the outfield, in addition to designated hitter Andrew Benintendi. Braden Montgomery is a switch hitter. They had right-handed outfielder Derek Hill earlier this season but traded him to the Phillies when righty Everson Pereira returned from injury.</p><p>Adams has ascended quickly this season, moving from rookie ball to High-A Winston-Salem to Triple-A Charlotte. In nine games (seven starts) with the Knights, Adams has a 4.25 ERA with 36 strikeouts and 17 walks in 36 innings.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Michigan reports first 2 U.S. deaths in outbreak of cyclospora
entries.summary: <p>LANSING, Mich. (AP) — Two people have died in the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/cyclospora-produce-washing-tips-022730ccbc514e15b1f0021c47bf1b68" target="_blank" >cyclospora outbreak</a> in Michigan in the first confirmed deaths in the U.S. related to the microscopic parasite, state health officials announced Monday.</p><p>The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said both people had underlying health conditions that may have been affected by the intestinal illness and dehydration.</p><p>The department said it will not be providing additional information about the deaths.</p><p>The parasite infects food that has come into contact with human feces, most commonly when produce is irrigated or washed with contaminated water. When ingested, it causes intestinal illness marked by “frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.</p><p>Federal health officials have identified lettuce from Mexico served at Taco Bell locations in five U.S. states as a source of the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/cyclospora-michigan-lettuce-taco-bell-244196c6f2a1b17ed872ef245ca6868f" target="_blank" >widespread outbreak.</a></p><p>Overall, cyclospora cases have set a U.S. record. Since May 1, the CDC has received reports of more than 4,100 confirmed cases and is investigating more than 7,400 other likely cases in 41 states. Federal health officials have said other “brands, restaurants, retailers or distribution channels” could be tied to the outbreak as the investigation continues.</p>

entries.title: Miles de personas que perdieron beneficios de SNAP en Illinois recibirán $400 del estado
entries.summary: <p>Miles de personas que perdieron la asistencia alimentaria federal debido a la ampliación de las normas laborales recibirán un beneficio único de $400 a partir del sábado, según funcionarios estatales.</p><p>El programa Familias que Reciben Apoyo de Emergencia para el Hambre (FRESH) proporcionará apoyo a unas 100,000 personas en Illinois que fueron consideradas no elegibles para el Programa de Asistencia Nutricional Suplementaria, conocido como SNAP, a partir del 1 de mayo. El estado asignó $70 millones para el programa en el presupuesto aprobado este año, y se permite un beneficio de $400 por hogar.</p><p>El Congreso amplió las normas laborales para el programa SNAP para incluir a personas de 55 a 64 años de edad, veteranos y padres cuyo hijo menor tenga 14 años o más. Desde que esas normas entraron en vigor en Illinois, unas 148,000 personas han perdido la asistencia alimentaria, según el Departamento de Servicios Humanos de Illinois (IDHS), que administra el programa y también distribuirá los fondos de FRESH.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-630000" name="module-630000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En general, la participación en el programa SNAP en Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/07/30/illinois-registra-una-caida-del-16-en-la-inscripcion-en-snap-un-ano-despues-de-los-cambios-al-programa" target="_blank" >disminuyó un 16%</a> desde el verano pasado, cuando el presidente Donald Trump firmó la ley que reformó el programa.</p><p>Los hogares elegibles para el programa FRESH no tienen que solicitarlo, según funcionarios estatales. Los fondos se distribuirán a través de las tarjetas Link, que es la forma en que los beneficiarios de SNAP reciben fondos para comprar comestibles.</p><p>"En Illinois, aprobamos el programa FRESH para ayudar a proporcionar cierto alivio para las familias expulsadas de la asistencia alimentaria, pero ningún estado puede cubrir los recortes crueles e inminentes que puso en marcha el proyecto de presupuesto de Trump", dijo el gobernador JB Pritzker en un comunicado.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
entries.author: Elvia Malagón

entries.title: Bears training-camp report, practice No. 5: RB Kyle Monangai back in action
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ Monday training camp practice:</p><p><b>What happened</b></p><p>It was a run-heavy practice for their first day in pads, and coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> got his first look at an offensive line that’s working to come together amid changes at center and left tackle.</p><p>It’s still a competition at the latter position, and newcomer Jedrick Wills got a shot with the first team. Braxton Jones remains the favorite to win the starting job, but Johnson said Wills is “firmly in the mix.” Theo Benedet and Kiran Amegadjie are competing as well.</p><p><b>One-on-one fun</b></p><p>Before the Bears got into team drills, they ran one-on-ones and delivered some highlights as the wide receivers took on the defensive backs. Luther Burden made a tremendous catch against very good coverage from Tyrique Stevenson on a Caleb Williams pass deep down the right side, and Kalif Raymond shook Jaylon Johnson with a stutter step to beat him deep as well.</p><p></p><p><b>Monangai returns</b></p><p></p><p>No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai, who sustained a minor muscle injury the first day of training camp, was back and in full pads Tuesday. Johnson indicated it’s not a significant concern going forward.</p><p></p><p><b>What’s next?</b></p><p>The Bears will practice in pads again Tuesday at 8:30 a.m.</p>

entries.title: Indiana AG sues Merrillville for opposing potential ICE facility
entries.summary: <p>Indiana’s attorney general is suing a northwest Indiana community for opposing a potential immigration detention center.</p><p>Republican Attorney General Todd Rokita, a staunch supporter of President Donald Trump, filed the state lawsuit last week against the Town of Merrillville.</p><p>Rokita is citing a newly-enacted state law, called the Fairness Act, that prevents local sanctuary policies, mandates cooperation with federal immigration detainers and penalizes employers who knowingly hire unauthorized workers.</p><p>“We requested that Merrillville comply with state law and they refused, choosing instead to play games, effectively aid and abet criminal illegal aliens, and making the illegals’ evasion of justice a higher priority than the safety of taxpayers throughout the region,” Rokita said in a news release. “That’s illegal under Indiana law.”</p><p>In January, the Town Council of Merrillville adopted a resolution opposing the conversion of large industrial warehouses into U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing or detention centers. The town had been cited in a published report as being a potential site.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a The council refused.</p><p>Rokita has also sued or warned other government entities for blocking or restricting ICE officers, including the <a class="Link" href="https://indianapublicradio.org/news/2025/11/rokita-sues-school-district-for-blocking-ice-from-schools/" target="_blank" >Indianapolis Public Schools</a>, the <a class="Link" href="https://events.in.gov/event/092425-attorney-general-todd-rokita-warns-blocking-sheriffs-cooperation-with-ice-would-be-illegal-fuel-indy-crime-surge?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=State+of+Indiana" target="_blank" ><u>Indianapolis-Marion City Council</u></a>, and <a class="Link" href="https://events.in.gov/event/attorney-general-todd-rokita-investigates-potential-labor-trafficking-and-interference-with-federal-immigration-enforcement-in-monroe-county?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=State+of+Indiana" target="_blank" ><u>Monroe County</u></a>, where Bloomington is located.</p><p>Town Councilwoman Keesha Hardaway said she isn’t intimidated by Rokita’s threats.</p><p>“I just feel as if this violates our First Amendment right on freedom of speech. We represent 5,000 residents each and we are their voice, and he is trying to squelch the voices of the town of Merrillville, and I will not tolerate that,” Hardaway said.</p><p>In a statement, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said it had no new detention centers to announce in Merrillville.</p><p>Lali Cuevas, founder of Northwest Indiana Community Response Team, said Merrillville is correct for opposing ICE in its town.</p><p>“People are already living in fear. Children not attending school, families unable to move about freely. And so with the detention center, that's really going to cause even more mistrust,” Cuevas said. "I hope they continue to stand their ground, even if you know fines do come. I know that's going to put a burden on the town. But I do feel like it should be a freedom of speech issue."</p><p>ICE facilities nationwide have also been places where inmates have alleged poor treatment and abuse, prompting Democrats in Congress to hold hearings.</p><p>Last week, the American Civil Liberties Union of Indiana filed lawsuits on behalf of an inmate at ICE’s detention facility at the Miami Correctional Facility, north of Indianapolis, nicknamed the “Speedway Slammer.” The inmate suffered a seizure after not receiving prescribed medication at the facility, then was pepper-sprayed by correctional officers.</p><p>According to Indianapolis TV station <a class="Link" href="https://www.wishtv.com/news/politics/aclu-reviews-merrillville-lawsuit/" target="_blank" ><u>WISH</u></a>, the ACLU is reviewing the lawsuit filed against the town by Rokita for possible violations of the First amendment.</p><p>U.S. Rep. Frank J. Mrvan, a Democrat who represents northwest Indiana in Congress and who is up for re-election this year, opposes ICE in the town and blasted the Trump administration for not consulting local officials, including himself.</p><p>"I respectfully call on the Administration to reverse any decision to convert commercial buildings for the purpose of detaining individuals in our district,” Mrvan wrote in a statement.</p><p><i>Michael Puente is a reporter and anchor for WBEZ. Reach him at mpuente@wbez.org.</i></p>

entries.title: Sky center Kamilla Cardoso taking patient approach to expanding her range
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> center <b>Kamilla Cardoso</b> has thrived in the paint this season. The bread and butter of the offense is finding her down low — off a pick-and-roll, a post-up or anything else that gets her the ball deep.</p><p>Saturday's win over the Aces gave Cardoso a taste of the bounty that lies beyond it. Most teams leave her wide open on the perimeter, and she finally made one pay, sinking her second jumper of the season to keep the game within reach.</p><p>If she took those more often, it would stress defenses even further and open up a new dimension for the Sky's offense. But Cardoso isn't in a rush to get there.</p><p>"I always want to improve my game," she told the Sun-Times last week. "I don't want to force anything. Whenever it's time, it's gonna come. I don't wanna go out there and start jacking up mid-ranges, because that's not what I do. I think it's gonna come."</p><p>The foundation is already in place. Cardoso's form is sound — her free-throw percentages reflect that — and she works on her jumper regularly before and after practice.</p><p>Coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> said she has the green light from him, though she’s still not taking many jumpers in scrimmages. He’s taking a patient approach, too. </p><p>"It's a comfortability thing for Mil," Marsh said. "It's not something we're discouraging. She does shoot it well when she has the time and space to do so.</p><p>"I think that 'Mil likes playing in her comfort zone. She's also been extremely effective around the rim. We want to continue to put pressure on the rim and utilize her in the areas where she's most effective."</p><p>And as tantalizing as adding range might be, it’s not unreasonable for her to master the paint first. She's converting 62.8% of her shots at the rim — a top-10 mark in the league and a significant leap from her first two seasons.</p><p>For now, Cardoso is locked in on the team's primary goal: the playoffs.</p><p>"For you to be in the playoffs, you gotta win games, and I think we've been working hard," Cardoso said. "We know what we gotta do to get there in the playoffs."</p><h3><b>Closing time</b></h3><p>Closing out games burned the Sky in the first half of the season. So their first week of practice back from the break was built around end-of-game scenarios, repped out again and again. Marsh emphasized not fouling on defense, and getting the ball in the right hands on offense.</p><p>He believes beating the Aces at the buzzer did a lot for morale — and that these nail-biters aren't going anywhere.</p><p>"Games are just that much tighter," Marsh said. "Teams are on their third and fourth time playing each other, so there's not that much disparity between them. So you got to execute down the stretch. All we can do is learn from our previous experiences from good or bad and be able to apply them moving forward."</p><h3><b>Standing by Stevens</b></h3><p>Forward <b>Azura Stevens</b> is still away from the team for personal reasons, with no timeline for a return.</p><p>"We've been in communication with her but we were not trying to press the issue," Marsh said. "We want to be sensitive to what she has going on. She knows that we're here to support."</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" entries.title: CPS told parents the start of school could be affected by budget changes. Experts say that’s unlikely
entries.summary: <p>Claiborne Wade was troubled when he woke up Friday morning to an email from the head of Chicago Public Schools telling parents like him that the school board had made a last-minute change to the budget that could affect the start of school.</p><p>At the time, Wade, a parent leader at the nonprofit advocacy group Kids First Chicago, wondered if most parents were even aware of the budget overhaul. It happened at night, after a marathon meeting, when “parents were getting ready for dinner, getting their kids ready for bed,” he said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/media/community-updates/2026/july/budget-update/" target="_blank" ><u>In her message</u></a>, Supt. Macquline King warned that the district may not be able to get the short-term loan it needs to make payroll, “which would effectively shut down the district just as staff and students are set to return.”</p><p>“My goal as a leader is to always be transparent, and it’s only fair that I be honest with you about where we are,” King wrote.</p><p>The message was dire, but even experts who are critical of the budget changes say it’s likely CPS will be able to borrow the money it needs and King sounded the alarm about a consequence that won’t play out. Still, they say it’s possible the changes, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>board members hope will rescind about 1,000 staff layoffs</u></a>, could lead to midyear disruptions, especially if the state doesn’t come through with the extra $150 million the school board is now counting on.</p><p>“I suspect CPS will come up with a way to limp along so that the front end of the school year starts and continues as planned,” said Joe Ferguson, the president of The Civic Federation, a fiscal watchdog that keeps tabs on the district’s finances. But Ferguson said given how “uncertain and unstable” the situation is, there’s a “legitimate and real concern about where this all goes.”</p><p>Why King made the assertion that the start of school could be interrupted is complicated.</p><p>One board member told WBEZ they thought King sent the alarming letter to families because she was upset that her budget was altered.</p><p>Rather than approve the budget King presented, board members assumed the state would provide more money — a move district officials warned was illegal and in violation of board members’ duties.</p><p>On Friday, the 11 board members who voted for those budget changes sent King a letter “respectfully asking her” to communicate financial risks “responsibly.” And they took the unusual step of laying out four things they wanted to see communicated.</p><p>The board members said King should refer to the budget as balanced — though King and her staff made it clear they don’t agree with that — and they wanted her to assure parents that the district has a plan.</p><p>In a statement, a CPS spokesperson said the district’s leadership would review that letter and continue to work with the school board.</p><p>In her letter to parents, King wrote that the newly amended budget relies on additional funding from the state that “CPS has not yet, and may not ever, receive.”</p><p>That money is up in the air. Illinois House and Senate leaders recently expressed support for giving CPS more money, but no specifics have been discussed. Similarly, on Friday Gov. JB Pritzker acknowledged state education funding is “not yet where we need to be” but said he is “a big believer” in balanced budgets.</p><p>King’s letter to parents centers on a concern that she and her acting financial chief, Wally Stock, share. They said an unbalanced budget could make creditors wary of giving CPS a loan. Without the loan and without the ability to pay staff, King and her staff are unsure that they can compel people to work.</p><p>CPS has taken short-term loans to cover payroll for many years, but it is in an especially bad financial position at the moment because <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/19/property-tax-payment-delay-costs-chicago-public-schools-almost-a-quarter-million-dollars-a-day" target="_blank" ><u>Cook County has been late disbursing property taxes</u></a> and expects to be late again.</p><p>Arnie Rivera, a former CPS official who is now the executive director of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/01/09/chicago-education-alliance-seeks-to-bring-clarity-to-cps-toughest-issues" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Education Alliance, an advocacy group</u></a>, agreed with Ferguson that CPS will likely be able to find a lender.</p><p>But Rivera said he suspects that there are not as many lenders as school district officials would like there to be, which means the cost of borrowing is high.</p><p>CPS paid $42 million to take out short-term loans to cover payroll last year. Even before last week, the district had planned to spend another $27 million in interest on short-term loans this year.</p><p>Justin Marlowe, the director of the University of Chicago’s Center for Municipal Finance, said that lenders are still open to CPS. He has interviewed CPS lenders as part of his work.</p><p>Lenders<b> </b>“are really only concerned with the revenues that are going to be used to repay” the short-term loans, he told WBEZ earlier this month. “As long as you know it's the property tax distribution from the county, the investors know that those dollars are coming.”</p><p>The school district “pre-commits” incoming property tax dollars to pay back the loans, and that’s sufficient as the “sole source of the pledge on these bonds,” Marlowe added.</p><p>In the meantime, parents like Wade are caught in the middle.</p><p>Wade said he understands that board members faced a difficult choice: approve a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/15/cps-will-cut-teachers-and-five-student-non-attendance-days-as-district-looks-to-close-budget-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>budget with layoffs that no one wants</u></a> or assume more money from the state and fight to get it — even if that seems unlikely.</p><p>Wade, who chairs <a class="Link" href="https://kidsfirstchicago.org/fully-funding-chicago-public-schools" target="_blank" ><u>Kids First’s equitable funding task force</u></a>, said parents are worried that their schools will not be adequately staffed.</p><p>Now he wants CPS leaders to put pressure on state lawmakers to take action to avoid midyear layoffs.</p><p>“I'm hopeful and optimistic that the state will do what it has to do in order for that not to happen,” Wade said. “The state needs to help.”</p>

entries.title: Notre Dame, USC will resume football rivalry with a 4-game series starting in 2030
entries.summary: <p>The Notre Dame-Southern California college football rivalry will start again in 2030.</p><p>The schools announced Monday they have agreed to a four-game home-and-home series. Notre Dame will play in Los Angeles on Aug. 31, 2030, and the Trojans will visit South Bend, Indiana, on Aug. 30, 2031. The meetings in 2032 and 2033 will be played in the first three weeks of the season.</p><p>The teams met each non-pandemic season from 1946-2025, typically in October or November, in what became known as "the greatest intersectional rivalry in college football." The exception was the 2020 season when most schools played a conference-only schedule.</p><p>Negotiations for the continuation of the series became challenging after USC joined the Big Ten in 2024. The Trojans expressed that they did not want to play nonconference games after September. Notre Dame beat the Trojans 34-24 in South Bend last Oct. 18, and the series officially went on hiatus in December when the Irish announced they had filled the last open spot on their 2026 schedule with a game at BYU.</p><p>Notre Dame and USC first played in 1926 and the Irish lead the series 53-38-5. The series also was put on hold from 1943-45, during World War II.</p><p>The two schools have combined to win 22 national championships and produce 15 Heisman Trophy winners, and the discontinuation prompted consternation on both sides. Navy is the only team Notre Dame has played more than USC, at 98 meetings.</p><p>Notre Dame and USC play for the Jeweled Shillelagh Trophy, a tradition which began in 1952. The Jeweled Shillelagh Trophy is presented by the Notre Dame Club of Los Angeles. Notre Dame victories are marked by green-jeweled shamrocks while USC victories are marked by ruby-jeweled Trojan heads.</p><p>"USC's historic rivalry with Notre Dame holds a special place in the history of college football, and we are happy to resume a series that means so much to the entire Trojan Family," USC athletic director Jen Cohen said. "It remains important for us to play this game early in the season, as it allows us to schedule competitively with our Big Ten peers and takes into account the health and best interests of our student-athletes and program. We are excited for our fans, and we look forward to more memorable matchups and unforgettable games between the Trojans and the Irish."<br></p>

entries.title: Baggu sets opening date for Lincoln Park store
entries.summary: <p>Baggu announced the opening date of its second Chicago store.</p><p>The California-based bag and accessories brand will open its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/04/07/cult-bag-brand-retailer-baggu-open-second-chicago-store" >Lincoln Park store</a>, 2118 N. Halsted St., on Aug. 14, according to an Instagram post from Baggu last week. The 2,200-square-foot space was previously home to It’s A Secret Medspa. </p><p>When Baggu opened its first Midwest store in Wicker Park in 2024, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2024/10/25/hundreds-shoppers-wait-line-among-first-inside-viral-brand-baggu-wicker-park" target="_blank" >hundreds lined up</a> to get inside on the first day. At the time, Baggu Director of Retail Stephen Stananhan said Chicago was its third largest market. </p><p>The brand’s new location is in a highly trafficked retail and dining corridor. The shop is also about two blocks away from the CTA Armitage L stop, where trendy retailers like Buck Mason and Gorjana have outposts.</p><p>The Lincoln Park store will be the brand's eighth location. It recently opened a store in Portland, Oregon, which joins five other locations in California and New York, as well as its Wicker Park store<b>.</b></p><p>Baggu has surged in popularity in recent years, leading to a brick-and-mortar expansion. Its reusable grocery bags in unique prints, often done in collaboration with other artists or brands, are particularly beloved by Gen Z.</p><p>Its reusable shopping bag, which can fold into a small pouch, starts at $16. Most bags and purses are made from nylon, although recycled leather purses, starting at $90, have returned in recent years. Other products include socks, toiletry bags and glasses cases, at prices ranging from $10 to $46.</p><p>Baggu didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2024/10/25/hundreds-shoppers-wait-line-among-first-inside-viral-brand-baggu-wicker-park" >Hundreds wait in line to be among the first inside viral brand Baggu’s new Wicker Park store</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: 60 años después de que Martin Luther King Jr. marchó en Marquette Park, cientos conmemoran su legado
entries.summary: <p>Bernice King contempló a la multitud portando ponchos y paraguas la mañana del sábado, haciendo eco de los llamados de su padre, que había estado en el mismo lugar 60 años atrás.</p><p>El reverendo Martin Luther King Jr. y otros activistas marcharon hacia Marquette Park en agosto de 1966 para protestar contra el “redlining” —una práctica inmobiliaria racista— y la discriminación en la vivienda que se extendió en Chicago en las décadas después de que poblaciones negras migraran al norte del país y se establecieran en la ciudad durante la Gran Migración.</p><p>Aquel día en Marquette Park, King y sus acompañantes fueron recibidos por turbas de blancos anglosajones enfurecidos que lanzaban piedras y cócteles molotov.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ac0000" name="module-ac0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Este año, Bernice King se unió al alcalde Brandon Johnson, al rapero originario de Chicago Common y a cientos de manifestantes para conmemorar el 60.º aniversario de la marcha, reiterando que la lucha por la justicia racial continúa décadas después.</p><p>Bernice King recordó al público lo que su padre denominó las “tres plagas” de la pobreza, el racismo y el militarismo.</p><p>“Siguen vivas, siguen mutando, siguen amenazando a nuestras comunidades", dijo. "Se esconden bajo nuevos disfraces, aparecen en políticas que castigan a los pobres y en sistemas que vigilan a los vulnerables, en estructuras que sacrifican la humanidad por el lucro".</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-19d0aa" name="image-19d0aa"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1ed3391/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5630x3160+0+297/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fde%2F03b1cac846ab9178975b3d0342d2%2Fmlkanniversary-260801-24.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c77d8b0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5630x3160+0+297/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fde%2F03b1cac846ab9178975b3d0342d2%2Fmlkanniversary-260801-24.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8c82260/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5630x3160+0+297/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fde%2F03b1cac846ab9178975b3d0342d2%2Fmlkanniversary-260801-24.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Bernice King, hija del Rev.
