Martin Luther King Jr., habla en Marquette Park tras marchar en Chicago Lawn el sábado 1 de agosto de 2026, donde la gente se reunió para conmemorar el 60.º aniversario de la marcha de Martin Luther King Jr. en Marquette Park contra la segregación.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Cientos de manifestantes desafiaron la llovizna y se congregaron en la intersección de la calle 63rd St. y Kedzie Boulevard antes de dirigirse hacia el sur, rumbo al parque, al son de cantos de protesta, consignas y enérgicas trompetas y tambores. Algunos llevaban camisetas con la leyenda "Sixty years later, we’re still marching" (Sesenta años después, seguimos marchando), mientras escuchaban a los oradores avivar a la multitud con historias de resistencia negra y llamados a la acción.</p><p>Common se presentó junto a la cantante Mumu Fresh y un grupo de coristas, aportando un tono góspel al acto mientras la gente vitoreaba y alzaba los puños.</p><p>En sus palabras, Bernice King contó que era una niña pequeña cuando su familia vivió en Chicago en la década de 1960 y les suplicaba a sus padres que la dejaran marchar con ellos. Se dirigió a la multitud y los instó a seguir afrontando las injusticias, señalando a la administración del presidente Donald Trump y a las autoridades federales de inmigración por el aumento de arrestos y deportaciones, la brutalidad policial contra las personas de color y la supresión del voto.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: 8 acts our reviewers loved at Lollapalooza
entries.summary: <p>Lollapalooza 2026 opened with warm sunshine on Thursday but the weekend soon brought rain and turned Grant Park into a mud pit.</p><p>But neither winds nor rain nor Saturday’s delayed start prevented our critics from canvassing stages in search of the next big talents. After all, veterans of Lollapaloozas yore like to compare notes on which major acts they saw way back when, be it Lady Gaga or <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2026/08/01/review-charli-xcx-delivers-jaw-dropping-drama-amid-made-for-movies-downpour#:~:text=theme%20Friday%20night.-,Charli%20xcx%20performs%20on%20the%20T%2DMobile%20stage%20at%20Lollapalooza,Friday%2C%20July%2031%2C%202026.&text=The%20ground%20pulsed%20as%20Charli's,the%20crowd%20to%20dance%20hard." target="_blank" ><u>Charli xcx</u></a> with early-in-the-day slots before making it big.</p><p>Here are 8 up-and-coming performers that our reviewers say will stay on their radars for months to come — and could end up on bigger stages in the future.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Cruz Beckham</b></h3><p>Cruz Beckham got his first taste of the stage 18 years ago. His mom Victoria Beckham, aka Posh Spice, was performing with the Spice Girls at Madison Square Garden, and the then-3-year-old<a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KoZ7a_nCPLQ&t=5s" target="_blank" ><u>busted out breakdancing</u></a> in front of 20,000 people, prompting Posh to declare him the “next Justin Timberlake.”</p><p>That he is not. But as Beckham and his band The Breakers made their festival debut at Lollapalooza on Sunday, he showed he could be the next great Brit rocker.</p><p>No one probably would’ve guessed that the 21-year-old (the youngest son of Posh and soccer legend David Beckham) would have one of the breakout sets of the weekend with an honest-to-god talent that supersedes his last name. Lollapalooza has opportunistically booked rock progeny before — Lars Ulrich’s sons in the band Taipei Houston and Travis Barker’s son Landon are recent ones that come to mind — and while both of those acts were just fine, Beckham doesn’t exactly follow the same lineage.— <i>Selena Fragassi</i>,<i> read the full review </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2026/08/02/review-cruz-beckham-and-the-breakers-lollapalooza" target="_blank" ><i><u>here.</u></i></a></p><p></p><div class="Enhancement" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>The Braymores</b></h3><p>The thing you gotta love about Chicago music fans is we’ll always show up for our own, whether it’s Lincoln Hall or Lollapalooza. The Braymores can now claim both after christening the BMI Stage Thursday for a larger-than-expected crowd, a few people appropriately wearing Cheap Trick and Smashing Pumpkins shirts.</p><p>The indie rock band hails from Barrington: “Close enough, it’s the same thing, right?” singer Matt Tilles bravely posited, surprisingly to little dissent. The quartet of high school friends who reconnected in 2022 grew up going to Lollapalooza. That heritage came through in their set. It swirled with ‘90s Wicker Park rock edge, hazy surf rock that brought Twins Peak vibes and a pride that can only come from playing the biggest music event in your backyard.</p><p>“This is the best day of our lives,” said Tilles. In addition to a homegrown crowd they’ve carefully cultivated in recent years, some of the band’s mothers appeared to be in the mix, recording the set with their phones and mouthing lyrics to songs like “Where Did My Baby Go,” “Like the Others” and “August,” the latter from their just-released album “When the Lights Went Out.”</p><p>The band also had time for a solid cover of Dr. Dog’s “Where’d All the Time Go” before wrapping. While their time at Lolla was short, The Braymores won’t be far this summer, headed back to another local stage at House of Blues Aug. 21. <i>– S.F.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8d0000" name="image-8d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7d0ffdb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F8f%2F140186104ae89eb0a93f461049e0%2Flollapicsday4-260802-14.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf6126b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F8f%2F140186104ae89eb0a93f461049e0%2Flollapicsday4-260802-14.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/95dc426/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F8f%2F140186104ae89eb0a93f461049e0%2Flollapicsday4-260802-14.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Destin Conrad performs at Allianz stage on Day 4 of Lollapalooza in Grant Park, Sunday, August 2, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/95dc426/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F8f%2F140186104ae89eb0a93f461049e0%2Flollapicsday4-260802-14.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/add6813/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F8f%2F140186104ae89eb0a93f461049e0%2Flollapicsday4-260802-14.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/95dc426/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F8f%2F140186104ae89eb0a93f461049e0%2Flollapicsday4-260802-14.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Destin Conrad performs at Allianz stage on Day 4 of Lollapalooza in Grant Park, Sunday, August 2, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Destin Conrad</b></h3><p>When discussing his Grammy-nominated debut album, “Love on Digital,” with Billboard, Destin Conrad called the sound “loud” and “queer.” Those are also fitting descriptors for his set on the Allianz stage at Lollapalooza on Sunday. But you could also add “unapologetically Black.”</p><p>The 26-year-old Florida native demonstrated his deep understanding of multiple Black art forms, performing R&B tracks from the aforementioned “Love on Digital,” and jazz tunes from his new album, “wHIMSY,” Oh, and he can also make irresistible island music; he played a song from his upcoming reggae album.</p><p>That versatility, along with his humor and natural performance ability onstage, is why he’s such an exciting new talent.</p><p>At the end of the set, the sun emerged from the clouds, as if to herald the rising of a new star. And by the lyrics of his song, “So Nice,” Conrad knows it, too. “It's OK, it's all right/My life is so nice.” <i>— Erica Thompson</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4f0000" name="image-4f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d7a0117/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F9a%2F1a2c3b784b59b953b8faf72a897a%2Flollapicsday3-260801-057.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8a18c91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F9a%2F1a2c3b784b59b953b8faf72a897a%2Flollapicsday3-260801-057.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2b95648/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F9a%2F1a2c3b784b59b953b8faf72a897a%2Flollapicsday3-260801-057.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Die Spitz fans do circle pits near the Airbnb stage on Day 3 of Lollapalooza in Grant Park, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. There was no in between.</p><p>When doors finally opened at 3 p.m. after rain delays, attendees scrambled to get through long security lines to make it on time for their preferred group. Both artists kicked off the festivities shortly thereafter and wrapped quickly after.</p><p>Those who made it to Die Spitz were greeted with their next feat: dealing with an overwhelming amount of mud swamps. While some froggered their way around them, others dived right in. “Girl pit! Girl pit!” chanted a growing group of women who formed a circle pit right in the thick of the sludge, clearly inspired by the ferocity of the four women on stage. Hailing from Austin, Die Spitz is the poster child for everything being bigger, bolder and brawnier in Texas. The group’s breakneck blend of riot grrl punk and heavy metal has already drawn comparisons to scene setters like Black Sabbath, Nirvana and L7, prompting Jack White to sign them to his Third Man Records label. And all this before most members turn 25.</p><p>“We’re really sad we have such a short set today but we’re really lucky we get to play,” said singer/guitarist Eleanor Livingston, making note of the many acts that were sacrificed to the weather gods Saturday.</p><p>The quartet worked with the 30 minutes they had, making a solid first impression before heading off to Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival later this month. But it wouldn’t be a shock to see them back at Lolla — on a bigger stage — in the near future, where they’ll hopefully get a proper full play. <i>— S.F.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Amber Mark</b></h3><p>“Someone’s getting fired” was the consensus after Amber Mark endured egregious microphone issues at the top of her set on the Allianz stage. The 32-year-old singer was clearly ready for her moment in the spotlight, looking like a true disco queen as she ascended the stairs of the stage-within-the-stage, which had been decorated with silver fringe. But the moment she opened her mouth, nothing. It went on like this for a few minutes until Mark and her band caught up with the crowd screaming, “Fix her mic!”</p><p>These snafus are always one of the pitfalls in an uncontrollable outdoor festival environment, but it couldn’t have happened at a worse time or for a more deserving artist.</p><p>Lollapalooza was a big moment for Mark, who recently came back to the stage after suffering a vocal fold hemorrhage that forced her to cancel previous tour dates. But the singer handled it all in stride, and once the issue was finally<i> </i>resolved, she was flawless.</p><p>Mark nailed covers of Prince’s “I Feel For You” and Michael Jackson’s “Wanna Be Startin’ Somethin’” and brought out the club vibes with “All the Work” after asking the crowd, “Do y’all like house music?” As if you even need to ask that question in Chicago.</p><p>By the end, Mark was on her knees, hands raised in prayer mode, thanking the heavens – and the crowd — for allowing it to work out in the end. “Thank you all so much for sticking through the technical difficulties,” she said, “we got through it.” —<i> S.F.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9a0000" entries.title: Hospitalizations up, arrests down across 4 days of Lollapalooza
entries.summary: <p>Ten people were arrested at this year's Lollapalooza, and 67 attendees were taken to nearby hospitals over the course of the four-day music festival that draws tens of thousands to Grant Park each summer, city officials said Monday. </p><p>That's fewer arrests and more ambulance trips compared to last year's festival, according to figures from Chicago's Office of Emergency Management and Communications. </p><p>Twelve people were arrested last year for a range of charges: theft, trespassing, reckless conduct and drug-related offenses. Forty-two people were hospitalized last year, which was the lowest recorded number in at least six years, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/08/04/lollapalooza-chicago-crime-arrest-grant-park-hospital" target="_blank" >officials said at the time</a>. </p><p>At this year's festival, the arrests were nearly evenly split across Thursday, Friday and Saturday. No one was arrested on Sunday, according to OEMC. The details of the arrests have yet to be released.</p><p>Over one-third of the hospital transports — 22 — happened on Friday. The fewest happened on Sunday, with only 11 people picked up by ambulances, OEMC reported. </p><p>A representative for Lollapalooza did not immediately respond to a request for comment. </p>

entries.title: In break from tradition, Thunderbirds to return to Chicago’s Air and Water Show for second year straight
entries.summary: <p>The U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds will return for a second consecutive year to this month’s Air and Water Show in Chicago, the city’s cultural affairs department announced Monday.</p><p>Historically, the Thunderbirds and U.S. Navy Blue Angels have traded off years appearing at the Chicago show, which regularly draws upwards of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-culture/2025/08/13/2025-chicago-air-water-show-golden-knights-thunderbirds-headliners" target="_blank" ><u>1 million spectators</u></a> to the city’s lakefront</p><p>The city said the break in tradition, which was first reported by <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/u-s-navy-blue-angels-unlikely-to-headline-2026-chicago-air-and-water-show/3943903/" target="_blank" ><u>NBC Chicago</u></a>, is due to a scheduling issue on the part of the Blue Angels.</p><p>“This year, the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds were available to participate, while the U.S. Navy Blue Angels had existing commitments,” a spokesperson for the target="_blank" ><u>America’s 250th birthday.</u></a></p><p>During a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/08/18/sonic-booms-lake-view-thunderbirds-chicago-air-water-show" target="_blank" ><u>Thunderbirds practice</u></a> for last year’s show, residents in Lake View heard booms that they described as an “earthquake” and “a massive jolt.” An expert told the Sun-Times that videos showed what were “clearly sonic booms,” the loud sound that occurs when a plane exceeds the speed of sound. The Air Force denied that any plane went supersonic.</p><p>That day, windows also shattered at a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/08/15/lakeview-apartment-windows-shatter-from-jets-practicing-for-air-and-water-show" target="_blank" ><u>Lake View condo building</u></a>, where residents said they felt strong vibrations as the jets flew overhead.</p><p>A similar event also previously occurred with the Blue Angels. In 2021, a Navy pilot <a class="Link" href="https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/will-blue-angels-perform-sneak-pass-in-new-bigger-jets-at-this-years-seafair-the-stunt-caused-problems-in-california/" target="_blank" ><u>caused more than $180,000 in damage</u></a> during a practice run after veering off course and nearing the speed of sound in California, according to The Seattle Times.</p><p>The Blue Angels also <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/navys-blue-angels-low-flyover-pensacola-beach-florida-video/" target="_blank" ><u>recently made headlines</u></a> for flying at a low altitude over a crowded beach during a show in Florida. In response, Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao wrote on X, “No reprimands. No firings. No problem. That's the sound of Freedom!”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3f0000" entries.title: Johnson blasts mayoral rival Giannoulias without naming him
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson charged Monday that the same billionaire business interests that closed schools and mental health clinics under former Mayor Rahm Emanuel are trying to “take us back to a time of trauma and torment” and declared that Chicago is “not going back.”</p><p>Johnson never mentioned Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias by name. But on the day after Giannoulias entered the race with a promise to confront the thorny issue of school closings, Johnson used the comment to his political advantage.</p><p>A previously planned announcement of the 15 more “sustainable community schools” bankrolled by the new teachers contract allowed Johnson to contrast his vision for Chicago Public Schools with Giannoulias’ tough-love message.</p><p>Sustainable community schools operate as comprehensive community centers that combine education with an array of social services for students and their families.</p><p>Johnson noted that the 15 choices “primarily service people of color and families who are in a social-economic strain right now that Donald Trump has exacerbated.”</p><p>That’s why, he said, he’s more focused on “protecting Chicago” than on mayoral politics and the lingering question of whether he will wage, what will almost certainly be an uphill battle for a second-term or walk away after four years in office.</p><p>“Right now, you have people who are declaring their candidacy for offices while already giving the word that they’re gonna close schools. The same interests that shut down schools,” Johnson told reporters at Malcolm X College.</p><p>“The same interests that closed mental health clinics. The same interests that fired working people across this city. Those same interests want to take us back to a time of trauma and torment and pain. I want to make this absolutely clear — and not just about sustainable community schools: We are not going back, Chicago.”</p><p>During a wide-ranging interview with the Chicago Sun-Times last week, Giannoulias condemned as “dangerously irresponsible” the Chicago Board of Education’s decision to approve a nearly $10 billion budget that counts on $150 million from Springfield that it doesn't have and a $285 million tax increment financing surplus that the City Council has not approved.</p><p>He accused schools members aligned with the Chicago Teachers Union of having "jammed through" an alternative budget that "avoids any hard choices about structural changes."</p><p>“I will work with the board president to advocate for more funding. But we have to start with a more responsible budget. ... Glittery possible revenue is not responsible," he told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Giannoulias also vowed to close some of the 145 schools with more empty seats than students, but with a community- and parent-driven process “paired with real investment in students and staff affected — not closures imposed from Downtown with little notice.”</p><p>“Past closures, particularly in 2013, were handled in a way that broke trust with Black and Latino communities, and that history can’t be ignored or repeated,” Giannoulias said.</p><p>Giannoulias’ remarks — and the $22 billion that he has raised from some of the same millionaire and billionaire business interest that bankrolled Emanuel’s two mayoral campaigns — provided a political opening for Johnson — and the mayor took it.</p><p>He firmly declared that the "days of school closures, consolidation and privatization ... ended officially under the Johnson administration."</p><p>"We have come too far to have the same interests that have created pain and turmoil in this city to try to take back seats or positions of power that, when they had it, they didn’t even use it for the benefit of working people,” Johnson said.</p><p>“They used these positions to fatten the pockets of the ultra-rich," he said. "They are carrying the same agenda of the Trump administration that released the largest upward transfer of wealth in the history of America. And none of those politicians said a word.”</p><p>When a caravan of buses was descending on Chicago during the $639.6 million migrant crisis, Johnson said he alone made the difficult choices and paid a political price for decisions that reignited an us-versus-them conflict between Black and Hispanic people.</p><p>“Who stood up for people in this city? My administration stood up for this city when there were no solutions across this globe of how to respond to a global population shift and migrants being shipped to create political turmoil,” the mayor said, his voice rising.</p><p>“I stood firm, 10 toes down. Even when it upset people, we took the humanitarian stance — not the political stance. And too many politicians in this city, in this state, are taking the stances and the interests of corporations.”</p><p>Giannoulias hopes to blunt some of those attacks by joining the mayor in campaigning for a 3% tax on annual income over $1 million.</p><p>But that's not enough to satisfy Johnson. </p><p>At a time when "too many politicians" are doing the bidding of corporations, the mayor said it has to be "yes to anything and everything" that makes Chicago the "safest, most affordable big city in America."</p><p>"Unless someone has that message, they are not fit to lead this city or anything else for that matter," he said.</p>

entries.title: Guardians strengthen rotation, offense as they chase White Sox in AL Central
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — The Cleveland Guardians made three trades Monday to bolster their lineup and surprisingly their rotation as they seek a third consecutive AL Central title.</p><p>Cleveland acquired All-Star pitcher Foster Griffin from the Washington Nationals for four players, strengthening one of baseball's top rotations. The Guardians also made moves to get outfielder Jo Adell from the Los Angeles Angels and first baseman Nathaniel Lowe from the Cincinnati Reds.</p><p>The Guardians (57-56) have been over .500 for most of the season, but are 6-10 since the All-Star break, tied for the third-worst mark in the American League. They are three games behind the first-place <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> in the AL Central and have a one-game lead over Minnesota for the league's final wild-card spot.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/03/white-sox-acquire-braves-catcher-joey-bart-wholl-play-for-his-third-team-this-year" >White Sox acquire Braves catcher Joey Bart, who’ll play for his third team this year</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/03/white-sox-get-outfielder-brenton-doyle-from-rockies-for-two-prospects-including-pitcher-mason-adams" >White Sox get outfielder Brenton Doyle from Rockies for two prospects, including pitcher Mason Adams</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The 31-year-old Griffin — tied for fourth in the majors with 12 wins — had emerged as Washington's ace after three years in Japan with the Yomiuri Giants. The left-hander is 12-3 with a 3.06 ERA and 116 strikeouts.</p><p>Guardians starters have a 3.68 ERA, sixth in the majors. Gavin Williams is second in the big leagues in strikeouts (178) and third in innings pitched (139), while rookie teammate Parker Messick was selected to the All-Star Game.</p><p>The Nationals received left-handers Will Dion and Josh Hartle, outfielder Nick Mitchell and right-hander Kendeglys Virguez in the deal.</p><p>Adding a couple more bats was a necessity for the Guardians, who have been offensively challenged the entire season. Cleveland has the third-worst batting average in the majors at .231, has scored the second-fewest runs (446) and ranks 27th with 109 homers.</p><p>The 27-year-old Adell adds power and some outfield versatility. He has 16 homers and 62 RBIs this season, one year after hitting a career-best 37 homers with 98 RBIs. Adell had spent his entire career with the Angels after being the 10th overall pick in the 2017 amateur draft.</p><p>The Angels received minor league catcher Jacob Cozart in the deal.</p><p>Lowe, 31, is batting .266 with 12 home runs and 37 RBIs. Rhys Hoskins and Kyle Manzardo have split time at first base in Cleveland, but Hoskins is batting .179 and Manzardo .215.</p><p>The Guardians traded right-hander Alejandro Rivera for Lowe. They also sent infielder Juan Brito to the Reds for cash.</p><p>To make room for Lowe on the 40-man roster, the Guardians transferred right-hander Shawn Armstrong to the 60-day injured list.<br></p>

entries.title: High-ranking Chicago police supervisors push to unionize amid beef with City Hall
entries.summary: <p>A group of high-ranking Chicago police officials are pushing to form their own union, setting up a possible fight with Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration.</p><p>In a letter last month to Militza Pagán, Johnson’s deputy mayor of labor relations, an attorney with the Illinois Police Benevolent & Protective Association asked the city to “voluntarily recognize” a new collective bargaining unit of police commanders and deputy chiefs. The union already represents sergeants, lieutenants and captains.</p><p>The union attorney, David Amerson, noted Chicago’s “long and proud history of being a pro-union city” and pointed to an executive order Johnson signed in 2023 expressing his commitment to “expand the right to organize for all Chicagoans.”</p><p>A source with knowledge of the unionization push said it was launched after the city curtailed how much time exempt-rank supervisors can spend on medical leave. </p><p>The issue only surfaced when two commanders were told they needed to return to work, as one remained hospitalized with a serious illness and the other was recovering from back surgery, the source said.</p><p>Commanders and deputy chiefs used to be able to tap into a year of medical leave, like other sworn department members. Now, they must accrue medical time at a rate of one day for every month worked, according to the source.</p><p>However, a mayoral spokesperson insisted there has been no change in policy.</p><p>"The Mayor’s Office met with the PBPA [Illinois Police Benevolent & Protective Association] in mid-July to gain an initial understanding of the issues facing Deputy Chiefs and Commanders and discuss their position," the spokesperson said in a statement. "The Mayor’s Office looks forward to continuing these conversations with Deputy Chiefs and Commanders, the PBPA, and leadership from the Chicago Police Department." </p><p>Commanders and deputy chiefs aren't afforded other benefits that other rank-and-file cops get, including earned time-off, pay for being prepared to work during off-hours and allowances for uniforms, the source said.</p><p>Lieutenants are now turning down promotions to become commanders because of the disparities — something that never used to happen, the source said.</p><p>“If you have an organization as large as ours, you need good leadership at the top in order to effectively run the department,” the source said. “And I have a big fear that we are going to get the complete wrong people, and the good people — the right people you want in those positions — are just turning it down.”</p><p>If Johnson’s administration doesn’t recognize a bargaining unit composed of commanders and deputy chiefs, the police supervisors plan to take their case to the Illinois Labor Relations Board and argue that a 2022 amendment to the state constitution gives them the right to unionize.</p><p>The board certified a bargaining unit of deputy district chiefs from the Chicago Fire Department in February. Fire battalion chiefs and Chicago Public Schools principals are among the other supervisors that can also unionize.</p><p>If the police commanders and deputy chiefs fall short at the labor board, they could then sue.</p><p>In an interview, Amerson said “the biggest benefit of collective bargaining is it professionalizes the service.”</p><p>“We used to have, in Chicago and across the state and across the country, patronage models for who could be a police officer,” he told the Sun-Times. “You better know the ward boss, you better know the alderman if you want to be a police officer.</p><p>“We moved away from that in the '70s [and] '80s and became a professionalized service, and I believe collective bargaining enshrines that. It removes the ideas of nepotism, favoritism, politics, so to speak, from advancing through the ranks. And it just generally encourages professionalism and civil service over patronage and political favor.”</p><p>Almost all commanders and deputy chiefs have supported the effort to form a union. The source said it’s “the right thing to do to build good leadership in the department.”</p><p>“It’s not about, OK, we’re crying because we don’t get paid enough,” the source said. “It’s, we’re crying that there’s not gonna be a good bench ready to go as things move forward.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/16/chicago-police-union-fop-misconduct-discipline" target="_blank" >Battle over Chicago police disciplinary hearings moves to state Supreme Court</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/04/01/chicago-police-staffing-study-larry-snelling" target="_blank" >Top cop bullish on study calling for hundreds of more officers — but unions, lack of money could stand in way</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Tom Schuba

entries.title: Pitchfork Festival co-founder settles lawsuit against him
entries.summary: <p>Organizers of the Pitchfork Music Festival have settled a lawsuit against the festival’s co-founder after accusing him of misappropriating more than $500,000 in festival funds.</p><p>Pitchfork Festivals LLC <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/10/pitchfork-music-festival-sues-co-founder-claiming-564k-in-festival-funds-alleging-misappropriated" target="_blank" ><u>sued co-founder Mike Reed</u></a> last month in federal court in Chicago, alleging he kept $564,680 by falsely claiming the money reimbursed expenses he had already incurred while preparing for the 2025 festival, which was later <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2024/11/11/pitchfork-music-festival-wont-return-in-2025" target="_blank" ><u>canceled</u></a>.</p><p>In a social media post shared Monday, Reed said he and Condé Nast — Pitchfork’s New York-based parent company — had reached a settlement.</p><p>"I want to thank the many people who have shown support over the last few weeks," Reed wrote on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DblcE85kdKz/?img_index=1" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>. "I’m happy to say that both parties have decided to settle our issues amicably. We can now put these issues in the past and move forward."</p><p>In a lawsuit filed July 6, Pitchfork accused Reed of fraud, unjust enrichment, breach of fiduciary duty, conversion, accounting and fraudulent transfer. </p><p>After the festival was canceled in 2024, and after a failed attempt to restart the event in 2025, organizers said they asked Reed to return nearly $4 million dollars that had been sent to his production company, Big Stik LLC. But Reed falsely claimed that more than a half million dollars had been used on labor and other fees when it hadn't, according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Instead of returning the funds, Reed allegedly transferred the money from the company contracted by Pitchfork to another entity under his control, At Pluto Ltd.</p><p>The lawsuit alleged that Reed concealed the transfer of funds and that Pitchfork only discovered it through the discovery process in a related arbitration proceeding.</p><p>Neither Reed nor Condé Nast immediately responded to a request for comment.</p>
entries.author: Cindy Hernandez

entries.title: Illinois state trooper accused of sexual assault in Tinley Park
entries.summary: <p>An Illinois State Police trooper has been charged with sexually assaulting someone in southwest suburban Tinley Park.</p><p>Douglass Lee, 54, of Tinley Park, is accused of assaulting a person who was “unable to give knowing consent” early Sunday, according to a statement released Monday by the Tinley Park Police Department. </p><p>Police did not share any additional details about what allegedly happened. Lee was expected to appear in court Tuesday on a criminal sexual assault charge in suburban Bridgeview.</p><p>Lee has been employed with Illinois State Police since January 2004 and is currently on administrative leave without pay, State Police said in a statement. </p>

entries.title: MLS hires Los Angeles FC co-owner Larry Berg to be next commissioner, succeeding Don Garber
entries.summary: <p>Larry Berg, co-owner of Los Angeles FC, will be the next commissioner of Major League Soccer, the league announced Monday.</p><p>At the start of the new year, Berg will take over for Don Garber, who has served as the league's commissioner since 1999.</p><p>The 60-year-old Berg, who will divest his ownership interest in LAFC, will be officially introduced on Tuesday at MLS headquarters in New York.</p><p>"I'm honored to lead Major League Soccer into its next era," Berg said in a statement. "Thanks to the vision and commitment of so many people, Major League Soccer has achieved tremendous success, but I believe our greatest opportunities are still ahead. We have an extraordinary opportunity to strengthen the quality of our competition, develop more world-class players, deepen our connection with supporters, and continue elevating Major League Soccer's place in the global game.</p><p>"Together with our owners, clubs, players, partners, supporters, and league staff, I could not be more excited for what comes next."</p><p>Garber will remain MLS commissioner through the end of the 2026 season before taking over as chairman of the league. MLS has grown tremendously during Garber's tenure, and hopes to capitalize on the momentum of the 2026 World Cup.</p><p>"Having worked closely with Larry over the past decade, I've seen firsthand the qualities that make him an exceptional leader, and I have complete confidence he is the right person to serve as Major League Soccer's next commissioner," Garber said in a statement. "His integrity, judgment, collaborative leadership, and unwavering commitment to building LAFC and the league have made him an invaluable partner. I look forward to working alongside Larry during this transition and supporting him as he leads MLS into its next chapter."</p><p>Berg previously held ownership stakes in Serie A club AS Roma, as well as Swansea City AFC in Wales. Under Berg's ownership, LAFC won the MLS Cup in 2022, and the Supporters' Shield in 2019.</p><p>Before he came to MLS, Garber was head of NFL International. In 1999, NFL team owners Lamar Hunt and Robert Kraft approached Garber and asked if he might be interested in serving as commissioner of the league, which was launched in 1996.</p><p>At the time Garber took over, the league was in trouble. By 2001 MLS appeared on the verge of folding, but Garber steered the league out of the crisis.</p><p>Under his watch, the league has expanded from 12 to 30 teams with the addition of San Diego FC in 2025. He introduced the league's marketing arm, Soccer United Marketing, encouraged the construction of soccer-specific stadiums and spurred the growth of an academy system to develop players in the United States.</p><p>Five clubs, Inter Miami, home of superstar Lionel Messi, LAFC, the LA Galaxy, Atlanta United and NYCFC are valued at over $1 billion, according to Forbes.</p><p>At the start, Berk will help guide the league as it shifts to a new summer-to-spring calendar to more align with its international counterparts. Currently the league plays a late winter to late fall schedule.</p><p>Following the conclusion of the current season, MLS will play a shortened 14-game "sprint season" in early 2027 before the league switches to its new schedule, kicking off in July with the league championship to be played in May 2028.</p><p>Last week in an interview with The Associated Press, Garber said it in was important for his successor to share the collective vision for the league.</p><p>"The next commissioner, I hope and expect, is going to believe in the future opportunity for our league and our clubs, and what role we can play domestically and internationally to grow the game and be responsible stewards for the game, and drive value for every stakeholder, every group that cares about their local club," Garber said.<br></p>

entries.title: Pearl Rieger, a lifeline to thousands of kids struggling with learning disabilities, dies at 98
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Pearl Rieger connected with kids in a way few can.</p><p>As a renowned educational diagnostician, she'd sit down with a kid, identify their obstacles to learning — such as dyslexia, ADHD or autism — chart a path forward, and work with parents and schools to implement it.</p><p>She helped thousands of kids in the Chicago area and beyond during a career that spanned nearly six decades. </p><p>Mrs. Rieger died July 23. She was 98.</p><p>"Her life's work was saving kids," former journalist Carol Marin said at Mrs. Rieger's funeral.</p><p>"I choke up because she saved my own kid," said Marin before recalling the moment she knew she needed to seek professional help for her son when he was in second grade.</p><p>"He was sitting on the steps in our house and he said, 'Mom, will you be mad at me if I quit school?' It was like a seven-alarm fire in my head and I talked to a friend who said 'You have to call Pearl Rieger, there's no one else, and she's very busy, she's booked day and night, see if she can fit you in, but you have to have Pearl Rieger.'"</p><p>Mrs. Rieger settled the boys nerves at their first meeting with the simple offer of "Let's get a cookie." </p><p>Mrs. Rieger maintained ties with the boy through his college years and became a close pal of Marin.</p><p>"It was Pearl who really helped (my son) and our family learn about his learning," said Marin said, who equated Mrs. Rieger's work to that of a lifesaver.</p><p>"She sees a kid in the middle of Lake Michigan drowning and with firm, strong, clear strokes, swims out and saves him," Marin said.</p><p>Mrs. Rieger was one of the founders of the Rush Neurobehavioral Center and a former advisor to Hyde Park Day School, which works with bright students with learning disabilities who weren't successful in traditional schools.</p><p>"She was a giant in the field," said Hyde Park Day School Executive Director Casey Crnich.</p><p>"You didn't want to get on the wrong side of her, if she believed in something, she believed in it very strongly and wasn't afraid to advocate for it. She was a force to be reckoned with," he said.</p><p>Attorney Matt Cohen, who advocates on behalf of families with children with special needs, said having Mrs. Rieger in your corner was a blessing.</p><p>"She was seen as the authoritative person on learning disabilities in both clinical and school communities, so when she was involved in a case where a child needed special services, the school would likely back off and do what she was recommending," Cohen said.</p><p>"She was also a leader in developing programming for kids with learning disabilities, so her impact wasn't just on individual children, it was also on how services were provided," Cohen said.</p><p>Mrs. Rieger entered the field in her 40s after divorcing her first husband, Dr. Edward Newman, a physician whose client list included Sammy Davis Jr., Henry Fonda and former Mayor Richard M. Daley.</p><p>"He wanted a trophy wife," said Mrs. Rieger's daughter, Nancy Halbeck. "But she wanted more."</p><p>Mrs. Rieger, who grew up in Hyde Park and had a degree in speech therapy from the University of Michigan, charted a new course by attending the University of Chicago where she earned a master's in educational psychology.</p><p>"She could have been a lady of leisure," Marin said. "But she worked."</p><p>She ran her practice from her home in the Powhattan residential high rise in Hyde Park and worked until she was 87.</p><p>"It was comforting for students to come into her home," said Peter Rastrelli, an educational psychologist who trained under and worked with Mrs. Rieger.</p><p>"The field has changed significantly over the years but you can still feel her influence here at our office, everything from the artwork and furniture to how you treat people and stay in touch as families need you to be available and how you communicate a child's story throughout their educational career," Rastrelli said.</p><p>Mrs. Rieger's second marriage to the late attorney Mitchell S. Rieger was long and happy. For many years the two liked to roll up their living room carpet, put on music, and dance together.</p><p>Mrs. Rieger was a regular visitor to Vail, Co., where she had a home, and skied well into her 80s. She also loved traveling with her grandchildren on special trips, including one to Vietnam.</p><p>A few of Mrs. Rieger's rules to live by included: When checking into a hotel you must jump on the bed to make sure that it is good, a lost car in a parking garage is not an inconvenience it's an adventure, keep floors clean so one can drop down and play cards, read a book or do a puzzle, and always put ketchup in a serving bowl, never bring the bottle to the table.</p><p>In addition to her daughter Nancy Halbeck, Mrs. Rieger is survived by her son Steven B. Newman, her daughter Mary Ann Moseley, and her stepchildren Karen Gross Cooper, Jill Levi, Linda Hanan, Susan Perlstein and Geoff Felsenthal.</p><p>Services have been held.<br></p>

entries.title: Ann Sather moving into shuttered Stella's Diner in Lakeview
entries.summary: <p>For six decades, Stella’s Diner served as a meeting ground for residents of the Lakeview neighborhood. Now, the diner's owner is selling the recently shuttered location to be converted into an Ann Sather Restaurant.</p><p>Owner Marvin Barsky told the Sun-Times that the sale of Stella's, at 3042 N. Broadway, was unrelated to the restaurant’s temporary closure earlier in July following a failed health inspection.</p><p>The reason for the sale, he said, was personal.</p><p>"I know people are thinking that we were closed and were forced out of business, but we weren't," Barsky said.</p><p>Barsky said the city later cleared the restaurant to reopen after the required corrections were made and some allegations were dropped. </p><p>The sale, he said, was in the works long before then.</p><p>"The restaurant was fine. We were open and operating, and everything was OK," he said. "Sadly for me, it was just time to go."</p><p>Barsky originally purchased the family-owned diner five years ago after returning from California to Chicago. He aimed to own a restaurant in the community he grew up in.</p><p>For Lakeview resident Annie Neyfakh, Stella's was woven into her childhood memories.</p><p>"I was really shocked that it was closing," Neyfakh, 25, said Monday. "That was my home restaurant. ... It's rough to hear the news."</p><p>The buyer of the property was Ann Sather Restaurants, another longtime Chicago staple led by former 44th Ward Ald. Tom Tunney.</p><p>Tunney said he was first approached by Barsky several years ago but initially declined the purchase offer because Ann Sather already operated nearby. That changed after his landlord asked the restaurant to leave its longtime flagship location, at Broadway and Roscoe, to make way for a neighboring business' expansion.</p><p>"We felt maybe now was the time to engage with Stella's and move the Broadway-Roscoe location to Broadway and Barry," Tunney said.</p><p>Tunney said the Stella’s will undergo renovations over the next couple months before reopening as Ann Sather. He hopes for an October opening.</p><p>"We're going to invest a fair amount of money in it," Tunney said. "Our plan is the same as always: Run a successful business that gives back to the community."</p><p>Barsky hopes customers remember Stella's for the decades it spent serving the neighborhood. He said many regulars have been stopping by to talk with him.</p><p>"They're all very curious, and a lot of them are very sad," Barsky said. "And I'm sad. But all of it was done, again, out of personal necessity — no other reason."</p>

entries.title: Illinois attorney general files lawsuit over Trump’s latest tariffs
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul on Monday sued the Trump administration for the third time over its latest efforts to impose tariffs, as part of a coalition of 23 state attorneys general.</p><p>The lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s decision last month to increase tariffs again.</p><p>“For the third time, I stand with my colleagues across the country to fight the Trump administration’s illegal tariffs. And we will continue this fight as long as the administration attempts to force its tariffs upon American consumers and businesses,” Raoul said in a news release.</p><p>The U.S. last month imposed taxes of 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 countries, accounting for 99% of U.S. imports, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.</p><p>The latest round of tariffs comes after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/02/20/supreme-court-trump-sweeping-tariffs-john-roberts-economic-agenda" >U.S. Supreme Court</a> in February ruled that some tariffs imposed by Trump last year were unconstitutional. In March, the U.S. Court of International Trade determined that companies subjected to tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/03/05/illinois-businesses-tariff-refunds-federal-court-trade" >entitled to refunds</a>.</p><p>“The Court of International Trade and the U.S. Supreme Court have already found the Trump tariffs to be unlawful, and we are confident we will prevail this third time,” Raoul said.</p><p>In Illinois, government agencies buy a range of imported products, or products made with imported components, according to a news release from Raoul’s office.</p><p>“And because the costs of tariffs are passed on the purchaser, those agencies face higher prices for the goods they have to purchase — price increases that will have to be paid with state tax dollars,” the release said.</p><p>Over the course of 2025, the average tariff rate on U.S. imports increased from 2.6% to 13%, according to researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The analysis from February found American consumers and businesses paid nearly 90% of the costs of tariffs last year.</p><p>Tariffs imposed last year drove small-business owners to take on new debt, tap into retirement savings and raise prices, among other measures, according to a national survey last month from grassroots group We Pay the Tariffs.</p><p>The survey of 241 businesses in 40 states, included three in Chicago: yarn store <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/23/we-pay-the-tariffs-survey-chicago-illinois-small-businesses" >Dropped Stitch</a>, incense maker Genieco and furniture seller Moderne Living.</p><p>Vernon Hills toymaker Learning Resources, which was part of the tariff lawsuit that won in the Supreme Court, filed a new lawsuit last month along with several other small businesses in the Court of International Trade over the current round of tariffs. The second lawsuit was filed by Burlap and Barrel, a New York-based spice company, and Collective Horology, a watch retailer based in Ventura, California.</p><p>“I applaud the Illinois Attorney General and the coalition of state attorneys general for standing up against the unlawful Sec. 301 tariffs. The attack on Rule of Law must end,” Richard Woldenberg, CEO of toymakers Learning Resources and hand2mind, said in a news release.</p><p>The coalition suing the Trump administration on its latest tariffs include the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin, as well as the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.</p><p><i>Contributing: AP</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/03/05/illinois-businesses-tariff-refunds-federal-court-trade" >Illinois businesses press for tariff refunds after a federal court ruled in their favor</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Cubs continue to bolster rotation, net Clay Holmes in swap with Mets
entries.summary: <p>A day after strengthening their rotation with a two-time All Star in Kevin Gausman, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> added another arm on trade-deadline day, landing Clay Holmes in a deal with the Mets.</p><p>Holmes, like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/02/dodgers-getting-tarik-skubal-only-makes-cubs-road-tougher" >Gausman</a>, was seen as one of the better pitchers on the trade block this summer. The 33-year-old right-hander hasn’t pitched since May, sidelined with a fractured fibula. He’s made three minor league rehab starts in the last week and a half as he works his way back to a big league mound.</p><p>Before the injury, Holmes had a stellar 2.39 ERA in nine starts. He was strong for the Mets last season, too, with a 3.53 ERA in 31 outings, 30 of them starts.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-moises-ballesteros-trade-deadline-angels" >Cubs upgrade bullpen with Ryan Zeferjahn, give up Moises Ballesteros in trade with Angels</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>He was twice an All-Star as a reliever, in 2022 and 2024, when he pitched for the Yankees. He logged 165⅔ innings in his first season as a big league starter last year.</p><p>Holmes steps into a Cubs rotation that looks much different than it did just 24 hours earlier. The additions of Gausman and Holmes to a group that already includes lefties Matthew Boyd and Shota Imanaga, both performing very well at this point in the season, figure to give them a wealth of options heading toward October.</p><p>The Cubs also boast lefty David Peterson, another trade acquisition from the Mets who has been quite effective in all but one of his starts since arriving, and will soon get righty Edward Cabrera back from a lengthy stay on the injured list. Righties Javier Assad and Colin Rea have been positive contributors as fill-ins during an injury-heavy campaign, and they figure to provide value as depth options.</p><p>This team knows how valuable that depth can be, stretched to its limits this season and fresh off depth issues helping them to an earlier-than-hoped playoff exit last fall. The Cubs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-moises-ballesteros-trade-deadline-angels" >acquired righty Braxton Garrett </a>from the Marlins as part of their trade-deadline activity, sending him to the minors as yet another depth piece.</p><p>Landing Holmes — and outfielder Tyrone Taylor — came at a cost, as the Cubs parted with infield prospect Jefferson Rojas to make the deal happen. Rojas, playing at Double-A Knoxville, was ranked as the team’s No. 2 prospect and the No. 63 prospect in baseball overall.</p><p>After balking at the high cost of pitching at last year’s deadline, team president Jed Hoyer showed no such conservatism this time around, trading away six of the organization’s top 30 prospects — and young slugger Moises Ballesteros — in a flurry of deadline deals.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Seven more beluga whales set to leave shuttered Canadian aquatic park as rescue operation continues
entries.summary: <p>Seven beluga whales were expected to leave Marineland Canada Monday, a little less than two weeks after four<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/22/belugas-chicago-shedd-aquarium-marineland-canada-rescue" target="_blank" ><u> arrived at Shedd Aquarium</u></a> from the shuttered aquatic park.</p><p>All seven belugas are headed for SeaWorld in San Antonio, said Andrew Burns, a longtime advisor and lawyer for Marineland. A group of four <a class="Link" href="http://u.ss" target="_blank" ><u>U.S</u></a>. and one Spanish aquarium, including Shedd, has agreed to take all 30 Marineland belugas, and the plan is to ship them all out by Aug. 31.</p><p>“The water gets lowered, then everybody prepares for the move and then they get picked up and moved,” Burns said Monday.</p><p>As many as six more could be on their way to Shedd. Burns had no information Monday about when those whales might be set to leave Marineland.</p><p>“We’re confirming that over the next little while,” he said.</p><p>Johnny Ford, a Shedd spokesman, said: “Details and timelines for additional rescues are expected to shift based on the needs of the animals and will not be shared in advance with the public, to ensure the safety of the animals and the people involved.”</p><p>Four belugas, all females, arrived at Shedd July 21 from Marineland, and Shedd officials have said they are<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/animals/2026/07/23/first-look-belugas-shedd-aquarium-whales-canada-trip" target="_blank" ><u> settling in well. </u></a></p><p>Marineland, located in Niagara Falls, Ontario, has been closed to the public since 2024. The financially strapped park had threatened to euthanize its 30 belugas if new homes couldn’t be found. Burns told the Sun-Times last month that the belugas were at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/23/canadian-belugas-rescue-shedd-aquarium-imminent-risk-lawyer-marineland" target="_blank" ><u>“imminent risk”</u></a> of being euthanized.</p><p>If the seven belugas leave Monday as expected, 17 more will remain at Marineland.<br></p>

entries.title: Durbin debe rechazar proyecto de ley que ampliaría la autoridad de ICE
entries.summary: <p>“Debemos frenar los abusos de ICE antes de que se pierda otra vida”, dijo el senador Dick Durbin, demócrata por Illinois, <a class="Link" href="https://www.durbin.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/durbin-statement-on-fatal-ice-officer-shootings-in-houston-and-maine" target="_blank" >el mes pasado</a> tras el asesinato de dos padres de familia, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo en Houston y Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero en Maine, a manos de agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p><p>La mayoría de los estadounidenses están de acuerdo con el sentimiento de Durbin de que ICE se ha salido de control, y así lo creen muchos de sus colegas en el Congreso. Ningún demócrata votó a favor de dar más fondos al Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) en junio.</p><p>Por eso es alarmante que Durbin haya respaldado otra iniciativa, Combating Organized Retail Crime Act o “<a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/opinion/congress-blog/homeland-security/5941947-combating-crime-act-backlash/" target="_blank" >CORCA</a>”, que empoderaría a DHS y a ICE a recopilar datos sobre compradores estadounidenses y ampliaría el alcance de la aplicación de la ley migratoria en nuestras comunidades.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c90000" name="module-c90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La industria del comercio minorista ha <a class="Link" href="https://www.grassley.senate.gov/news/news-releases/law-enforcement-and-retail-industry-leaders-call-on-congress-to-pass-the-combating-organized-retail-crime-act-through-the-ndaa" target="_blank" >ejercido una intensa labor de cabildeo</a> a favor de la ley, logrando apoyo bipartidista de miembros del Congreso que temen ser etiquetados como “blandos” con el crimen.</p><p>Sin embargo, tras conocer la ampliación de poder de ICE en este proyecto, 10 copatrocinadores demócratas en la Cámara optaron finalmente por no votar a favor. Ahora la propuesta se está preparando para debate en el Senado.</p><p>Sabiendo que la ley es indefendible en el fondo, el cabildeo está redoblando esfuerzos para colarla en la Ley de Autorización de la Defensa Nacional, un paquete legislativo de aprobación prácticamente obligatoria. El lobby ha publicado columnas de opinión por todo el país intentando presionar al senador de Nueva Jersey, Cory Booker, quien se ha opuesto a CORCA desde hace tiempo, así como al senador de Rhode Island, Jack Reed.</p><p>Durbin ha sido uno de los copatrocinadores principales de CORCA y apoyó incorporarla rápidamente y sin debate en la Ley de Autorización de la Defensa Nacional. Hacemos un llamado a él y a otros senadores demócratas para que rechacen este proyecto y sigan liderando la lucha por frenar a ICE.</p><p>Una amplia coalición de más de <a class="Link" href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1-L-BwH-bWChX7tGpew9EFSfHzoK95_cT/view" target="_blank" >130 grupos de derechos civiles, de reforma de justicia penal y de inmigración</a> —incluyendo la NAACP, la American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) y otros— instan a los senadores a que se concentren en soluciones reales para mantener a los estadounidenses seguros.</p><p>Durbin ha sido un opositor vocal de la expansión de la aplicación de la ley migratoria, incluso votando en contra de la Ley Laken Riley, que incrementó la autoridad de detención de ICE y que muchos senadores hoy lamentan haber apoyado.</p><p>Como líderes en derechos civiles, le instamos ahora a solicitar que CORCA se debata por sus propios méritos y a votar en contra.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.vera.org/people/insha-rahman" target="_blank" ><i>Insha Rahman</i></a><i>, presidenta, Vera Action </i><br><a class="Link" href="https://www.nilc.org/people/kica-matos/" target="_blank" ><i>Kica Matos</i></a><i>, presidenta, National Immigration Law Center </i></p><h3>Niños no acompañados pierden representación legal</h3><p>Los proveedores de servicios legales, que representaban a cerca de <a class="Link" href="https://acaciajustice.org/leaders-call-out-trump-administrations-move-to-strip-unaccompanied-children-of-legal-counsel/" target="_blank" >20,000 niños no acompañados</a> en todo el país, acaban de ser desfinanciados por el gobierno federal. Esto significa que los niños se verán obligados a presentarse ante un juez de inmigración sin abogado.</p><p>Mientras observaba una corte de inmigración en Chicago, vi a “Carlos”, de 12 años, de pie frente a un juez de inmigración. El abogado de Carlos le dijo al juez que el papá había pasado por el proceso de investigación del gobierno para lograr la liberación de su hijo, pero fue detenido y deportado —una práctica que la administración de Trump ha adoptado para cumplir sus cuotas masivas de deportación y lograr que los niños “abandonen” el país de forma “voluntaria”.</p><p>Los niños se usan como carnada, y los padres evidentemente se presentan a las audiencias con la esperanza de reunirse. ¿Quién no lo haría?</p><p>Seis meses después, Carlos y su abogado regresaron a la corte. El centro de detención donde había estado Carlos estaba cerrando. Su traslado a una nueva instalación era inminente. Esto reanudaría en parte el proceso de investigación y retrasaría aún más la liberación de Carlos o podría conducir a su deportación.</p><p>El abogado de Carlos pidió una extensión más. El fiscal del gobierno se opuso, pero el juez concedió sólo una semana más. Una semana después, Carlos fue entregado a su tía, una ciudadana estadounidense. El juez mostró evidente alivio.</p><p>La vida de un niño. El drama de una familia. Otro día más en la corte con niños detenidos.</p><p>¿Te imaginas si Carlos no hubiera tenido un abogado que abogara por él?</p><p>La administración de Trump está desmantelando la red de casi 100 proveedores de servicios legales que representaban a niños no acompañados como Carlos. El contrato para representar a estos niños, un programa bipartidista financiado desde 2003, terminó el 31 de julio.</p><p>Ahora decenas de miles de niños se enfrentan a la posibilidad de representarse a sí mismos en la corte. ¿Conoces a un niño de 12 años? Esto está mal.</p><p><i>Joy Olson, Milwaukee </i></p><h3>Aprende sobre los disturbios raciales de 1919</h3><p>Gracias al Sun-Times por publicar el artículo titulado <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/07/24/1919-chicago-race-riot-commemoration-project-peter-cole-franklin-dunni-cosey-gay-myles-francis" target="_blank" >“Remembering victims of 1919 Chicago race riot: 38 names set in stone”</a> (Recordando a las víctimas de los disturbios raciales de Chicago de 1919: 38 nombres grabados en piedra) el 25 de julio. Este es un hecho histórico importante, y es adecuado que haya sido memorializado con placas de piedra.</p><p>Para quienes quieran profundizar, recomiendo mucho el libro de 2018 <a class="Link" href="https://www.abebooks.com/9780358667995/Few-Red-Drops-Chicago-Race-0358667992/plp" target="_blank" >“A Few Red Drops: The Chicago Race Riot of 1919"</a> de Claire Hartfield. El libro examina los acontecimientos con gran detalle e incluye muchas fotografías —algunas difíciles de ver por su cruda realidad.</p><p>Vale la pena notar los paralelos históricos entre 1919 y hoy: la autora explica que las tensiones que alimentaron los disturbios se habían ido gestando durante décadas. Oleadas de inmigrantes blancos de Europa y migrantes negros del sur del país convergieron para formar una clase baja dividida por los prejuicios raciales. Esta animosidad racial fue explotada por los magnates que controlaban el mercado laboral, enfrentando a esos grupos entre sí.</p><p>¿No suena todo esto demasiado familiar? Hoy tenemos a inmigrantes latinos enfrentados a la clase trabajadora blanca anglosajona, una situación que sigue siendo explotada por Donald Trump y sus simpatizantes.</p><p>Y por eso nunca debemos olvidar estos hechos. Nos arriesgamos a repetir los mismos errores costosos, en perjuicio de la sociedad.</p><p><i>Bob Chimis, Elmwood Park </i></p><h3>La Ciudad empeoró las inundaciones</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/07/27/flooding-act-of-god-rundown-infrastructure-sewers-drainage-catherine-nakalembe" target="_blank" >Catherine Nakalembe</a> tiene razón: las inundaciones en Chicago son un fallo de políticas, no un acto de Dios. Yo iría más lejos. En algunos vecindarios, la Ciudad está destruyendo activamente las alcantarillas que se supone debe mantener.</p><p>Soy un ingeniero jubilado de alcantarillado de la Ciudad de Chicago. Este verano tuve 15 pulgadas de agua saliendo a chorros por el desagüe del piso y 18 pulgadas de aguas residuales en mi sótano. Contraté y pagué a un contratista privado para inspeccionar mi línea de desagüe y averiguar por qué.</p><p>El Departamento de Gestión del Agua había instalado una nueva tubería en nuestra cuadra. Para cumplir con los estándares de separación de agua y alcantarillado, cambiaron las tuberías privadas por hierro dúctil. Pero en lugar de reconectar mi desagüe donde siempre había estado, lo reconectaron 8 pies arriba de la conexión original, en contra del flujo de la alcantarilla principal. Mi casa ahora es una válvula de alivio para la alcantarilla principal. Eso fue lo que salió por mi desagüe.</p><p>No se detuvo en mi propiedad. A petición de nuestro concejal, también se inspeccionó la alcantarilla principal. Ese informe muestra tubería rota y vacíos bajo la calle: un daño nuevo a una alcantarilla principal de 12 pulgadas y 100 años de antigüedad que ya era insuficiente antes de que la tocaran.</p><p>Las solicitudes para corregirlo no han tenido resultado. Mi desagüe fue excavado dos veces antes de ser reparado, según el código.</p><p>La reparación no es complicada, solo cara. Colocar las conexiones donde pertenecen y reparar lo que se rompió, reemplazando la alcantarilla principal inadecuada de 12 pulgadas por tubería reforzada sobredimensionada, de 24 a 36 pulgadas.</p><p>En mi carrera municipal, exigíamos a los desarrolladores privados que detuvieran su agua de tormenta. La Ciudad debería exigirse ese mismo estándar y usar tubería sobredimensionada para contener la avalancha de agua en la calle en lugar de en nuestros sótanos.</p><p>Vivo a dos cuadras de un pozo del Deep Tunnel. Más capacidad en las tuberías del vecindario le daría a esa agua el tiempo que necesita para llegar al pozo.</p><p>Culpar a Dios es cómodo. Culpar al clima es cómodo. Ninguno de los dos es responsable de las inundaciones en mi sótano.</p><p><i>Edward Koehler, Ravenswood </i></p><h3>El cambio climático</h3><p>Estoy seguro de que miles de víctimas estadounidenses de inundaciones, incendios y tornados están contentas de saber que el presidente Donald Trump y la mayoría de los republicanos creen que el cambio climático es solo un engaño “woke”.</p><p><i>Robert Kleps, Oak Park </i></p><h3>Subrayar el valor de Medicaid y Medicare</h3><p>En un momento en que la atención médica a través de Medicaid y Medicare está bajo asedio constante, espero que sigan publicando cartas como la reciente columna de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/07/22/never-underestimate-medicare-value-property-tax-assessments-errors-global-warming" target="_blank" >Lequita Michelle Mayhew</a> en apoyo de esos programas beneficiosos y a menudo salvavidas.</p><p>Tras 40 años con seguro privado en el volátil mundo corporativo, pude jubilarme e inscribirme en Medicare. La estabilidad y la tranquilidad de saber que estoy cubierto son beneficios que no supe apreciar hasta necesitarlos. Antes, nunca sabía si mi empleador cambiaría de aseguradora, si las compañías subirían las tarifas o si mi empleador decidiría ahorrar reduciendo su contribución.</p><p>Según mi experiencia y la de muchos otros, creo que ha llegado el momento de un sistema nacional de salud de pagador único. Muchos gritarán “pero mis impuestos”, pero una vez que comprendan los beneficios netos, no querrán volver atrás.</p><p><i>John Hankes, Streeterville </i></p><h3>La difícil situación en la prisión de Joliet es inaceptable</h3><p>¿Qué determina si una sociedad se ha vuelto moralmente en quiebra? No soy experto, así que no puedo decirlo con certeza. Sin embargo, la investigación del Marshall Project, el Sun-Times y WBEZ sobre las condiciones en el <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/24/joliet-prison-fires-mental-health-illinois-department-corrections" target="_blank" >Joliet Treatment Center</a> es un caso bastante claro de que estamos lejos de donde debemos estar.</p><p>Cuando los presos están tan desesperados por ayuda que creen que la única forma de obtenerla es prenderles fuego a sus celdas y a sí mismos, todos deberíamos sentir repugnancia.</p><p>En lugar de lamentarnos por un impuesto a la propiedad más alto, ¿qué tal si permitiéramos que esos fondos adicionales ayudaran al Joliet Treatment Center? ¿Es más importante mantener nuestros estilos de vida, o debemos exigir que las personas invisibles para la sociedad no sean descartadas tan a la ligera, sin importar el costo?</p><p>Me parece extraño y desalentador que colectivamente aceptemos que quizás la población más vulnerable —reclusos con graves problemas de salud mental— viva en condiciones tan horrorosas.</p><p>Si necesitamos una razón egoísta para asegurar la vida de estos reclusos, deberíamos considerar que al asegurar que siempre se les trate como humanos, garantizamos que el resto de nosotros no se vuelva invisible. Este vergonzoso fracaso moral es nuestra responsabilidad, aunque dudo que, como sociedad, cumplamos con la obligación de proporcionar las necesidades humanas más básicas a los reclusos del Joliet Treatment Center.</p><p>Si esto no es una señal de la podredumbre moral en el centro de nuestra sociedad, realmente no sé qué lo sea.</p><p><i>Ethan Feingold, Lake View </i></p><h3>Consuelo frío</h3><p>Recordando oleadas de calor como nuestras recientes temperaturas abrasadoras, saludo y me solidarizo con todos los trabajadores que laboran en el exterior. Para techadores, cuadrillas de carreteras, jardineros, obreros de la construcción y otros, no hay forma de esquivar ese clima —solo aguantarlo. Esa es una dureza que no he tenido que igualar desde mis días de correr en competencia. Por suerte, las horas libres les ofrecen alivio adentro.</p><p>No fue así durante la Gran Depresión. Mi madre decía que en los peores tiempos, antes de que el aire acondicionado fuera algo habitual y la casa era un horno, la familia mojaba las sábanas en agua fría para envolverse antes de acostarse en el patio. Otros sacaban sus colchones afuera o se iban a los parques de Chicago. Y después de que bajaba el calor, se podía tardar tres días más en enfriarse el interior de los edificios.</p><p>Eso fue entonces, pero incluso ahora, nuestra empleada del hogar nacida en Polonia me cuenta que la mayoría de las viviendas europeas carecen de ese aparato inestimable que llamamos aire acondicionado.</p><p>¿A quién agradecer por esta bendición tan poco valorada? A un ingeniero de principios del siglo XX llamado <a class="Link" href="https://www.williscarrier.com/" target="_blank" >Willis Carrier</a>. Probablemente ni una de cada diez personas lo conoce, pero sin él el nivel de confort humano caería por completo. Y ni es recordado en su estado natal de Nueva York. Al menos yo no lo olvido. Cada vez que entro desde un infierno exterior a mi refugio con temperatura controlada, envío pensamientos positivos a don C., dondequiera que se encuentre.</p><p><i>Tom Gregg, Niles</i></p><p><i> </i><br><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
