entries.title: Chicago comic with da accent turns city’s municipal code into laughs in new podcast
entries.summary: <p>Musician and comedian Al Scorch thinks he got the “last gasp” of an old school childhood growing up in the 1980s and ‘90s on Chicago’s blue collar Northwest Side.</p><p>“Pre-cell phone, pre-internet … where you're just kind of running around the neighborhood in a pack with your friends all summer,” Scorch said. “You're coming home when the streetlights turn on. You're calling up your friends' houses on their landline.”</p><p>That “last gasp” was more like a deep inhale that shaped Scorch into a Chicagoan’s Chicagoan with an imaginative sense of humor and authoritative knowledge of the city. He’s been exhaling Chicago-centric creative projects that have gained him tens of thousands of followers in the decades since. Now, he’s embarking on a major endeavor: to read the entire municipal code of Chicago aloud for a podcast in an iconic Chicago accent.</p><p>The accent is an exaggeration of his own vernacular, honed in alleys and parks growing up with friends who would imitate the adults in their lives as comedic relief.</p><p>“It was this way of making fun of these adults who would be kind of jerks to us,” Scorch said. “You know they’d be like, ‘Don’t-ch-you kids go messin’ ‘round wit’ my garbage cans!’ And you're just like — that's the funniest thing I've ever heard.”</p><p>Scorch plans to release weekly episodes reciting the code, which governs everything from how tall you can grow your parkway plants to how the city defines bodily autonomy.</p><p>It’s Scorch’s latest in his catalogue of love letters to Chicago, from an Emily Dickinson-style <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/CuIpdvGOo1L/" target="_blank" >poem about hot dogs</a>, a 2015 get-out-the-vote video called the “<a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bAvqo3K1Sn4" target="_blank" >City Hall Shuffle</a>,” a series reviewing historic <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DYSSc9NOPTW/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==" target="_blank" >Chicago Park District bathrooms</a> in an iconic Chicago accent and now <a class="Link" href="https://open.spotify.com/show/6KRdWg6fonR1r5i8kTnHRr" target="_blank" ><i>Municipal - the code of Chicago</i></a>.</p><p>“It's part of being an artist in the city,” Scorch said. “Growing up here and staying here, it creeps into your creative work. All these characters I do are a part of me.”</p><p>In PDF form, the city code spans 3,205 pages, including the appendix, with any given page containing 1,300 words. At an average speed, reading it in full could take 32,050 minutes, or 534 hours, or 22 full days. Scorch has read about 115 minutes so far, but he is determined.</p><p>“When you're creative, there's a little bit of compulsion. You're like, ‘I had this idea, and I have to do it,’” Scorch said. “I thought, ‘I need to read the entire municipal code of Chicago aloud,’ so I guess I have to now.”</p><h3>Perfecting the accent</h3><p>On a recent afternoon, Scorch sets up his makeshift recording booth in the vintage clothing store he partially owns. It’s a folding table and a high quality microphone surrounded by railings of clothes that act as a sound buffer.</p><p>He’s working on Chapter 10-28, structures on and under public ways.</p><p>Flattening his vowels, flexing his nasal muscles, occasionally trading a “th” for a “d,” and adding some hissing “s’s,” he recites dry legalese on how to get a canopy permit.</p><p>“[T]hat the construction of such marquee or canopy shall … be subject to inspection by the Department of Buildings, and the permittee shall pay to the city all cost of such supervision and inspection,” Scorch reads.</p><p>The episodes are exactly this. No more and no less.</p><p>The podcast came to fruition after social media users raved about Scorch’s put-on accent that went viral in his reviews of Park District "bat-ch-rooms."</p><p>“My new sleep aid,” one user writes. “I find this soothing,” says another. “Whenever I miss my grandpa, I'll just come listen to you talk,” someone says.</p><p>Scorch wanted to give people a long-form way to listen and, as an artist, he saw the chance for a supplemental, recurring source of income. Some of the podcast is free on streaming services, but the rest is on Scorch’s paid Patreon account.</p><p>Listeners use his podcast to fall asleep, to relax, to remember home or to laugh.</p><p>Becky Clough is an assistant public defender who grew up in Beverly and listens to the podcast a couple times a week while doing office work, like writing case briefs.<b> </b>She says it helps her unwind, and she finds it nostalgic and funny.</p><p>“There's something that's, as a Chicagoan, so familiar about ‘a guy,’ right?,” Clough said.</p><p>“Like your dad or your uncle that's really into, say, cars, and you have one issue with your car, and you're in the alley and the garage door’s open and you just want this one thing fixed, but then they keep going and going and going … and then all of a sudden you know more about, like, your vehicle than you ever intended to. It gives me a little of that flavor,” she said.</p><p>Others, like Ald. Nick Sposato (38th) who oversees the Northwest Side area where Scorch grew up, have a different take on the project.</p><p>“I can't imagine many people watching that,” Sposato said in his own notoriously thick Chicago accent.</p><p>“I could see them watching the bathroom videos, but reading the entire municipal code? I don't know. Not something I could do.”</p><p>Asked if he thought Scorch’s accent sounds authentic, Sposato said: “I can't recognize these Chicago accents. Everybody tells me, ‘Nobody's got a Chicago accent like you.’ I'm like, ‘What accent are you talking about?’”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Comedian Al Scorch’s reviews of Chicago Park District bathrooms, highlighting the quality of building materials, drew raves from social media followers.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Mixing comedy and conscience</h3><p>While his bathroom reviews and his aspiration of reading the entire city code have garnered attention, Scorch is an accomplished recording artist and songwriter. He has a residency at the Hideout running through 2026.</p><p>And as any Chicagoan, Scorch is politically informed and engaged. He starts a recent social media post by jokingly saying, “Thanks everybody for laughing at all the stupid videos I make,” before asking viewers to buy tickets to an upcoming show that raised money for the Illinois Coalition on Immigrant and Refugee Rights.</p><p>“All these family separations and abject cruelty and horrendous treatment of human beings — they’re helping those families deal with it, so please come out,” Scorch said.</p><p>Scorch has also used his musical and comedic talent to weigh in on Chicago’s red-hot mayoral races. His 2015 music video promoted then-candidate Jesus “Chuy” Garcia in his race against incumbent Rahm Emanuel. He promoted Mayor Brandon Johnson over Paul Vallas in a similar 2023 video. He’s also behind the viral song “Paul Vallas Hates House Music.”</p><p>Scorch thinks Chicago's intrinsic politics behind the policies is what makes his podcast interesting.</p><p>“The civic government and the municipal body is such a part of Chicago culture, and it's a huge part of our identity,” Scorch said.</p><p>Reading the code, it’s easy to see how lobbyists have shaped laws or how ordinances have upheld systems of power and patronage, which he joked “really gets my dander up.” But it’s also a living document that’s constantly changing.</p><p>“At the worst times, [it’s] graft and quid pro quo and unfairness,” Scorch said.</p><p>“But it's also this beautiful, collective document of self-governance that has been updated and changed and rewritten by thousands of people over hundreds of years. … People can change it for the better.”</p>

entries.title: After Senate primary loss, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi shifts focus to new PAC — and his political future
entries.summary: <p>U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi is shifting his fundraising powers to a PAC to benefit other Democrats ahead of his own exit from Congress — a move that also gives him flexibility should he decide to run for office again.</p><p>Krishnamoorthi plans to hold a launch reception for a new hybrid-PAC called Equal Opportunity Now on Wednesday in the West Loop, according to a flyer obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. Federal Election Commission filings show the PAC had $2,369,758.26 cash on hand at the end of June. The congressman's Senate campaign fund still has $74,587.81 cash on hand.</p><p>A source familiar with the event said the PAC will announce contributions to a slew of state and Chicago candidates, with plans to contribute $100,000 to candidates this month alone. </p><p>"Although I'm not on the ballot, I still want to do my part to help Democratic candidates and causes at both the national and local level. This organization is laser-focused on supporting the leaders and causes that are championing bold and innovative solutions to defend the American Dream," Krishnamoorthi told the Sun-Times in a statement. "To me, this means ensuring that every American has the opportunity to receive a high quality education, work for fair wages, build economic security, and participate in a thriving democracy."</p><p>Those close to the Schaumburg Democrat say the PAC is a way for Krishnamoorthi, a prolific fundraiser, to use his talent and network to help down-ballot candidates. And despite a contentious primary, the congressman contributed $2,500 from his leadership PAC to primary rival Juliana Stratton in June after attended a Washington fundraiser benefiting her. </p><p>The new PAC also will keep him active in donor networks and could be helpful should he choose to run for Congress, or another office, again.</p><p>The Reviving American Jobs Act PAC, with the acronym RAJA, was created by Krishnamoorthi in 2017 as his leadership PAC, but has transitioned to the Equal Opportunity Now PAC. According to the PAC's website, Krishnamoorthi plans to "support ambitious leaders and causes who will do the hard work to fix the key challenges ailing Americans today." Priorities include many of his own campaign's platforms: fair wages, defending democracy and lowering the cost for working families. </p><p>A transfer of funds to a PAC after a loss is typical, with candidates able to legally transfer remnants into leadership PACs or political committees to help other candidates. </p><p>With Stratton poised to win the Senate seat in November, and Duckworth unlikely to leave anytime soon, Krishnamoorthi could potentially set his sights on another run for his House seat or try running in another district. He could also explore a run for Illinois governor in 2030. But for now, he's focusing on his exit from Congress after nearly nine years in office. </p><p>During his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/07/raja-krishnamoorthi-launches-senate-bid" target="_blank" >primary campaign for the Senate</a>, Krishnamoorthi raised more than $30 million and spent an astounding $29 million on campaign ads. He was largely viewed as a frontrunner of the race for many months. But Stratton's momentum — including a commanding debate performance, campaign ads and a financial boost from longtime running mate Gov. JB Pritzker — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/us-senate-illinois-primary-results" target="_blank" >helped put her over the finish line.</a> </p><p>Stratton’s results downstate reflected a much broader coalition than people expected and served as a testament of Pritzker’s popularity among Democrats in the state.</p><p>Krishnamoorthi led in the collar counties and also won a number of downstate counties, particularly in the northwest and western parts of the state — many places where the number of Democratic voters are dwarfed by those found in Cook County. Even so, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/18/juliana-stratton-us-senate-democratic-primary-victory-strong-showing-suburbs-downstate" target="_blank" >Stratton’s huge margin in Chicago</a> and slim margin in suburban Cook went a long way to propel her to victory.</p><p>Krishnamoorthi first won election in 2016 after losing two previous runs for elected office — finishing second to now-Sen. Tammy Duckworth in the Democratic primary for the 8th Congressional District in 2012, and losing the state comptroller race in 2010 by a slim margin. Krishnamoorthi currently serves as ranking member on the Select Committee on the Strategic Competition between the U.S. and the Chinese Communist Party and the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform's subcommittee on Health Care and Financial Services. He also serves on the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.</p><p><i>Contributing: Fran Spielman</i></p>

entries.title: Cubs upgrade bullpen with Ryan Zeferjahn, give up Moises Ballesteros in trade with Angels
entries.summary: <p>A day after addressing the top of their starting rotation and making a trade-deadline splash by landing veteran righty <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/02/dodgers-getting-tarik-skubal-only-makes-cubs-road-tougher" >Kevin Gausman</a>, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> upgraded their relief corps, bringing in 28-year-old right-hander Ryan Zeferjahn in a deal with the Angels.</p><p>It cost them one of their top young players, with slugger Moises Ballesteros going the other way in the trade.</p><p>Zeferjahn has been very effective this season, already logging 51⅔ relief innings and posting a 3.66 ERA. He’s been even better over the last couple months, with a microscopic 1.38 ERA in 24 appearances since June 1.</p><p>Zeferjahn is in his third big league season, his ERA down more than a full point from last season, when he made 62 relief appearances.</p><p>Zeferjahn was almost exclusively a late-inning option for the Angels. Since the start of May, he pitched earlier than the seventh inning only twice.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-trade-deadline-clay-holmes-mets" >Cubs continue to bolster rotation, net Clay Holmes in swap with Mets</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>For much of the season, injuries have forced the Cubs to piece together their bullpen, and their pitching staff in general. Injuries to expected contributors such as righties Phil Maton and Hunter Harvey and closer Daniel Palencia have forced unexpected arms into high-leverage roles, with righties Jacob Webb and Trent Thornton, as well as lefty Ryan Rolison, stepping into late-inning jobs.</p><p>Zeferjahn, who finished 17 games for the Angels this season, figures to join that late-inning group.</p><p>After hitting nearly .300 and reaching base at nearly a .400 clip in 2025, Ballesteros started this season with the expectation of playing a key, if not everyday, role for the Cubs. But his numbers weren’t nearly as good in limited playing time this time around, hitting .231 and posting just a .303 on-base percentage before being sent to Triple-A Iowa in mid-June to receive more regular at-bats.</p><p>In 32 games with the I-Cubs this season, Ballesteros hit just .235.</p><p>Also going the other way in the trade is pitching prospect Mason McGwire, son of legendary slugger Mark McGwire, who was rated as the No. 18 prospect in the Cubs’ organization.</p><p>The Cubs also made a move for a minor league starter, acquiring lefty Braxton Garrett from the Marlins in exchange for a pair of top-30 prospects. Garrett was immediately sent to Triple-A Iowa as a depth piece.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Review: Ado, Japan’s mysterious megastar, delivered the most metal performance of this year’s Lolla
entries.summary: <p>It’s entirely possible that in a few years we’ll find out Ado is just a front for a secret CIA operative.</p><p>Since coming on the scene in 2020, the real person behind the mysterious J-pop star has been kept up under wraps. Anonymity is a foundational part of her identity as a singer who started as a cover artist and rose to international fame through the community of creators using Vocaloid, a Japanese music-composition software. And the lengths Ado’s team goes to keep her identity secret is a mind-blowing feat and quite impressive in the age of social media.</p><p>Watching this process unfold at Lollapalooza was truly a marvel. Thirty minutes before Ado’s finale set at the Airbnb Stage kicked off, crews worked furiously to set up the large metal cage she performs behind — only visible as silhouette — while testing out a massive amount of lights strategically placed in front for another optical distraction.</p><p>Messages came across screens warning the throngs of people gathered that absolutely no photos, videos, recordings or binoculars of any kind would be allowed before, during or after the show. No one was really policing the demand, and it’s likely you can find snippets of the set on YouTube. At least we hope so, since Ado’s performance was one of the most intriguing of the weekend and it should be documented for posterity.</p><p>By now, Lollapalooza has become a musical IHOP — or, international house of pop. And Ado’s quote-unquote J-pop set capped off the festival’s global consonant trail, following on the heels of K-pop (Jennie, i-Dle, Aespa, Cortis) and P-pop (SB19). The only problem is there’s nothing really pop about Ado at all. In fact, she was one of the most metal things we saw all weekend.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Messages came across screens warning the crowd that absolutely no photos, videos, recordings or binoculars of any kind would be allowed before, during or after the show. Japanese megastar Ado performs at the Airbnb stage at Lollapalooza in Grant Park on Sunday, Aug. 2, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>While Ado was stuck behind her cage, an amplified four-piece band did a ton of showboating at the top of the stage, shredding their way through all 10 songs, accompanied by fireballs and laser light trickery. Ado also did just enough twirling and jumping to give proof of life to know her shtick is not just a ruse for some AI hologram.</p><p>Her powerhouse voice is nothing that could be manufactured, either. The way she was able to change from screaming to high-register singing on a dime, it could do laps with Rob Halford or Bruce Dickinson.</p><p>High points of the set came with “Usseewa,” “Kira” and the obvious “Rockstar.” All were done in Ado’s native Japanese, but the crowd devoured the songs nonetheless, waving around light sticks in her signature blue color and chanting her name throughout the brief 45-minute show. Ado also performed her rare English language song “Stay Gold” and did her best with a brief speech, too.</p><p>“Good evening, Chicago! I’m Ado, thank you for coming to my show tonight,” she began. “This is an amazing city. If I ever decide to move to America, Chicago is at the top of my list. And Chicago pizza, it’s yummy!”</p><p>She had more to stay but noted her teleprompter was having issues and switched over to speaking in Japanese. But no translation was needed to know what this moment meant to her and to the dedicated fans who felt an obvious connection, even if they have no idea who she is.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule
